title: Impact of Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger revealed by a single cosmic clock: thick-to-thin disc transition, gas disc shrinking and bar formation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Whether the formation of the Galactic bar was connected to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger, the last significant merger experienced by the Milky Way, remains an open question. The bar formation epoch has been inferred from the star formation history of the nuclear stellar disc (NSD) traced by Mira variables, and the GSE merger epoch from the age-metallicity relation of red giants. However, these epochs rest on different stellar tracers with different age scales and cannot be compared directly. We recalibrate the Mira period-age relation onto the age scale of APOGEE red giants, with ages from a Bayesian neural network trained on Kepler asteroseismic ages. We fit the Gaia DR3 proper motions of 2394 O-rich disc Mira variables with an action-based quasi-isothermal distribution function whose parameters vary with period, and derive the period-age relation by matching their vertical velocity dispersion as a function of period to that of the APOGEE red giants as a function of age in Funakoshi et al. (2025). This places the NSD star-formation rise and peak at 8.5-10.5 Gyr ago on the red giant age scale, overlapping with the final stage of the GSE-induced starburst, thick-to-thin disc transition and the contraction of the star-forming gas disc. If NSD star formation traces bar formation, these coincidences suggest a possible scenario in which the GSE seeded the bar formation, while fresh gas supplied by the GSE and outer disc gas driven inward by its tidal torques, increased the baryonic dominance of the inner Galaxy.

AI.tldr: Recalibrating the Mira period-age relation onto the APOGEE red giant age scale places the nuclear stellar disc star-formation peak at 8.5–10.5 Gyr ago, coincident with the final stage of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger, suggesting the merger may have seeded Galactic bar formation.
AI.motivation: The link between Galactic bar formation and the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger is unresolved. Bar formation epochs (from Mira-traced nuclear stellar disc star formation history) and the GSE merger epoch (from red giant age-metallicity relations) rely on different tracers and age scales, so they cannot be compared directly. A common age scale is needed.
AI.method: The Mira period-age relation is recalibrated onto the APOGEE red giant age scale, using ages from a Bayesian neural network trained on Kepler asteroseismic ages. Gaia DR3 proper motions of 2394 O-rich disc Mira variables are fitted with an action-based quasi-isothermal distribution function whose parameters vary with period. The period-age relation is then derived by matching the Mira vertical velocity dispersion vs. period to that of APOGEE red giants vs. age (Funakoshi et al. 2025).
AI.result: On the red giant age scale, the NSD star-formation rise and peak are placed at 8.5–10.5 Gyr ago, overlapping with the final stage of the GSE-induced starburst, the thick-to-thin disc transition, and the contraction of the star-forming gas disc.
AI.conclusion: If NSD star formation traces bar formation, these coincidences suggest a scenario in which the GSE seeded bar formation, while fresh gas supplied by the GSE and outer-disc gas driven inward by its tidal torques increased the baryonic dominance of the inner Galaxy.

title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: the delayed rise of Lyman continuum escape fractions in bursty high-redshift galaxies
comment: 26 pages, 24 figures. Comments welcome
summary: The ionizing radiation that galaxies release into their surroundings depends on whether efficient Lyman continuum (LyC) escape coincides with strong photon production. Stellar feedback can open escape paths as the source population fades, linking the escaping radiation to a galaxy's recent history. We investigate this timing in thirteen high-redshift (z > 3) target haloes from the THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, post-processed with COLT radiative transfer and sampled at ~10 Myr intervals. The clearest delayed relationship links $\text{SFR}_{10}/\text{SFR}_{100}$ to the LyC escape fraction. Selecting the nearest positive cross-correlation peak gives typical lags of ~16 Myr and peak correlations of 0.4-0.6 in massive haloes, with longer and less coherent delays towards lower masses. The fitted delays scale approximately as $M_\star^{-0.19}$ and $M_\text{halo}^{-0.27}$, although the shortest lags approach the native snapshot spacing. Recurrent variations span multiple amplitude-dependent timescales, consistent with repeated episodes of star formation and feedback. Recent star formation closely tracks both intrinsic and escaping photon rates, while the escape fraction reflects the evolving gas transparency. The H$α$-to-UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed association with escape, offering an observable connection between burst phase and leakage. High transparency during a fading phase can nevertheless yield little escaping radiation. The temporal overlap of photon production and transmission therefore shapes both the amount and timing of escaping radiation, informing the interpretation of observed leakers and their contribution to cosmic reionization.

AI.tldr: Using THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulations post-processed with COLT radiative transfer, the study finds a delayed (~16 Myr) positive correlation between the recent star-formation ratio SFR10/SFR100 and the LyC escape fraction in massive z>3 haloes, with delays scaling as stellar and halo mass and Hα/UV ratio offering an observable tracer of the burst-leakage connection.
AI.motivation: Galactic ionizing radiation output depends on whether efficient Lyman continuum (LyC) escape coincides with strong photon production. Because stellar feedback can open escape channels as the source population fades, escaping radiation may be tied to a galaxy's recent star-formation history, motivating an investigation of the timing between burst phase and leakage.
AI.method: Analyzes thirteen high-redshift (z>3) target haloes from THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, post-processed with COLT radiative transfer and sampled at ~10 Myr intervals. Cross-correlation analysis is applied, focusing on SFR10/SFR100 versus the LyC escape fraction, extracting nearest positive correlation peaks and fitting delay-mass scaling relations.
AI.result: The clearest delayed relationship links SFR10/SFR100 to the LyC escape fraction, with typical lags of ~16 Myr and peak correlations of 0.4–0.6 in massive haloes; delays are longer and less coherent at lower masses, scaling as M*^-0.19 and M_halo^-0.27 (shortest lags approaching snapshot spacing). Recurrent variations span multiple amplitude-dependent timescales. Recent star formation tracks intrinsic and escaping photon rates, while escape fraction reflects evolving gas transparency; the Hα-to-UV ratio retains a delayed association with escape. High transparency during a fading phase can still yield little escaping radiation.
AI.conclusion: The temporal overlap of photon production and gas transmission shapes both the amount and timing of escaping radiation. This informs interpretation of observed LyC leakers and their contribution to cosmic reionization, highlighting burst timing as a key factor alongside instantaneous escape conditions.

title: The black hole-galaxy correlations of the 12 micron local AGN sample: a NuSTAR perspective
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures (+ Appendix), accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: The M-sigma correlation of inactive galaxies plays a crucial role in estimating the black hole mass (MBH) in active galactic nuclei (AGN): 1) it is used to calibrate the reverberation mapping (RM) method; 2) the RM is the basis of the single epoch method, the most-used technique to determine MBH of broad-line AGN; and 3) in narrow-line AGN, MBH is often directly inferred from the M-sigma correlation. The main goal of this work is to test whether the M-sigma relation calibrated from inactive galaxies can be reliably applied to a local AGN population spanning Seyfert 1, Seyfert 2, and hidden broad-line region galaxies (HBLRs), and whether the resulting AGN relation has sufficient predictive power to be used as an indirect MBH estimator. To investigate this hypothesis, we used the 12 micron AGN sample, a local representative and largely unbiased sample. Since a substantial fraction of this sample has good-quality NuSTAR data, we estimated their MBH with the X-ray scaling method, which works for any AGN accreting at moderate or high level. We find that the M-sigma correlation of the 12 micron AGN sample is different from the one obtained with inactive galaxies and has a substantial scatter. Therefore, its predictive power for MBH estimates is fairly limited. We also find that the MBH-Mgal correlation based on the 12 micron AGN sample is consistent with the analogous correlation obtained from a large sample of nearby type 1 AGN and inconsistent with that of inactive galaxies. Finally, we find suggestive evidence that Seyfert 1 and HBLRs have similar and systematically higher Eddington ratios than Seyfert 2 galaxies.

AI.tldr: The M-sigma relation calibrated on inactive galaxies differs from that of a local 12-micron AGN sample and has substantial scatter, limiting its predictive power for black hole mass estimation in AGN.
AI.motivation: The M-sigma correlation of inactive galaxies underpins black hole mass estimates in AGN—it calibrates reverberation mapping, which feeds the single-epoch method, and is directly used for narrow-line AGN. Whether this calibration reliably transfers to local AGN (Seyfert 1, Seyfert 2, HBLRs) and offers sufficient predictive power is the central question.
AI.method: Using the local, representative 12-micron AGN sample, the authors estimated black hole masses via the X-ray scaling method, applicable to AGN accreting at moderate-to-high levels, leveraging the substantial NuSTAR coverage of the sample. They compared the resulting M-sigma and MBH-Mgal correlations against those of inactive galaxies and a large sample of nearby type 1 AGN.
AI.result: The 12-micron AGN M-sigma correlation differs from the inactive-galaxy relation and shows substantial scatter, giving fairly limited predictive power for MBH. The MBH-Mgal correlation agrees with that of nearby type 1 AGN but is inconsistent with inactive galaxies. Suggestive evidence indicates Seyfert 1 and HBLRs have similar, systematically higher Eddington ratios than Seyfert 2 galaxies.
AI.conclusion: Applying the inactive-galaxy M-sigma calibration to AGN is not reliably justified; the resulting AGN relation has limited value as an indirect MBH estimator. The MBH-Mgal and Eddington-ratio differences further distinguish AGN from inactive galaxies, with Seyfert type linked to accretion rate.

title: The LBT Y$_{\rm p}$ Project VI: Gas-Phase Chemical Abundance Patterns of Metal-Poor Nebulae
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal. Comments welcome
summary: Through a combined rest-optical and NIR observing campaign, the Large Binocular Telescope Primordial He Abundance ($Y_{\rm p}$) Project has delivered a precision measurement of $Y_{\rm p}$. Given the stringent requirements to measure gas-phase He abundances, the optical spectra contain emission features from a plethora of metals in the Interstellar Medium (ISM). We present gas-phase N, O, Ne, S, Cl, Ar, K and Fe abundance patterns in 62 low-metallicity nebulae. We assess ionization correction factors for each element and select those that reproduce the observed ionic abundance trends. The Ne/O, S/O, and Ar/O abundances do not evolve with metallicity and agree with the solar ratios. Given the Type Ia enrichment of S and Ar, the solar S/O and Ar/O suggest extended star formation histories in local galaxies relative to high-$z$ galaxies at fixed O/H. We report the first ISM K abundances in low-metallicity extragalactic nebulae; both Cl/O and K/O are constant with O/H, indicating the production of these odd-Z elements follows that of $α$ elements. Consistent with prior analyses, gas-phase Fe/O is observed to decrease with O/H due to dust depletion; correcting for this produces an average [Fe/O]$=$$-$0.80, implying Fe-deficient stars capable of producing hard ionizing spectra. Finally, the metallicity-insensitive log(N/O) plateau from 50 nebulae is $-$1.43$\pm$0.10, consistent with previous works. Five galaxies have N/O significantly enhanced relative to the primary plateau, and we discuss their properties, mechanisms that could bias measurements of N/O, and nucleosynthetic progenitors that can produce enhanced N at low metallicity.

AI.tldr: The LBT Primordial He Abundance Project measures gas-phase N, O, Ne, S, Cl, Ar, K and Fe in 62 low-metallicity nebulae, showing that Ne/O, S/O, Ar/O, Cl/O and K/O are metallicity-independent and solar-like, while Fe/O declines with O/H due to dust depletion, and deriving a primary log(N/O) plateau of -1.43±0.10.
AI.motivation: Precise He abundance (Yp) measurements require careful characterization of the metal emission lines contaminating optical spectra. Understanding the chemical abundance patterns and nucleosynthetic origins of these elements in low-metallicity gas is needed both to support the Yp determination and to constrain enrichment histories and dust depletion.
AI.method: Combined rest-optical and NIR spectroscopy of 62 low-metallicity nebulae. Ionization correction factors are derived per element and validated against observed ionic abundance trends. Abundance ratios relative to O are compared as a function of O/H and against solar ratios.
AI.result: Ne/O, S/O and Ar/O show no metallicity evolution and match solar; solar S/O and Ar/O, given Type Ia enrichment, suggest extended star formation in local galaxies at fixed O/H. First extragalactic low-metallicity ISM K abundances; Cl/O and K/O are constant with O/H, indicating odd-Z production tracks α-elements. Fe/O decreases with O/H from dust depletion; depletion-corrected average [Fe/O] = -0.80, implying Fe-poor stars with hard ionizing spectra. Metallicity-insensitive log(N/O) plateau = -1.43±0.10; five galaxies show significantly enhanced N/O, with discussion of measurement biases and low-metallicity N producers.
AI.conclusion: The metal abundance patterns in low-metallicity nebulae are consistent with α-element behavior for Ne, S, Ar, Cl and K, dust-driven Fe depletion, and a robust primary N/O plateau, motivating Fe-deficient stellar populations as sources of hard ionizing radiation and highlighting rare N-enhanced systems requiring further nucleosynthetic study.

title: Confirming candidate self-lensing binary detections with radial velocity measurements
comment: Submitted to RASTI
summary: Compact objects in approximately edge-on binary orbits with stars are able to produce a self-lensing effect, amplifying light from their companion once per orbit. To date, five white dwarf self-lensing systems are known, while none are known containing black holes or neutron stars. Discovery of such systems is a potential method of finding quiescent black holes and neutron stars, most of which will be pristine and unchanged from their formation. Photometric detections can suffer from degeneracies in the lens mass and orbital parameters when the amplification and crossing time are not well constrained, while photometric searches produce too many false positives to allow radial velocity investigation of every candidate. Therefore we investigate the minimal radial velocity (RV) observational requirements to characterise such systems by simulating detectable self-lensing light curves, using those light curves to generate targeted RV observations, and fitting RV jointly with photometry. We evaluate the median relative error in the recovered lens mass and orbital period, alongside compact-object class recovery. We find that adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter error, with compact-object class generally easier to determine than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems, with even a small number of RV measurements resulting in substantial improvement in accuracy. These results suggest that multi-stage RV follow-up, starting with a small number of observations of many candidates, can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for further investigation.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies minimal radial-velocity (RV) follow-up requirements needed to characterize self-lensing compact-object binaries, showing that even a small number of RV measurements jointly fit with photometry sharply reduces lens-mass and orbital-period errors and enables compact-object classification.
AI.motivation: Self-lensing in edge-on compact-object–star binaries offers a way to discover quiescent black holes and neutron stars, but only five white dwarf self-lensing systems are known and none with BHs/NSs. Photometric searches alone suffer mass–orbital-parameter degeneracies and produce too many false positives for RV follow-up of every candidate, so the minimal RV requirements must be established.
AI.method: Simulate detectable self-lensing light curves, use them to design targeted RV observation sets, and perform joint fitting of RV data with photometry. Evaluate median relative error in recovered lens mass and orbital period, plus compact-object class recovery, as functions of RV sampling, RV precision, and orbital period.
AI.result: Adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter errors; compact-object class is generally easier to recover than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by the number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems; even a few RV measurements yield substantial improvement.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage RV follow-up—beginning with a small number of observations across many candidates—can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for further investigation.

title: The PAU Survey: Active galactic nucleus galaxies in galaxy pairs
comment: 16 pages, 18 figures, accepted by A&A
summary: Aims. Leveraging the high-precision photometric redshifts of the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS), we aim to investigate the connection between active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and galaxy pairs up to redshifts of $\sim1.0$. Methods. We identified 16,824 galaxy pairs with projected separations of $r_p < 100$ kpc and radial-velocity differences of $ΔV < 3500$ km s$^{-1}$. AGNs were selected by cross-matching PAUS galaxies with multi-wavelength AGN catalogues, yielding 270 AGNs in pairs out of a parent sample of 8,880 AGNs in PAUS. We constructed control samples of isolated AGNs; non-AGNs in pairs; and isolated non-AGNs matched in redshift, absolute magnitude, and environment. Results. Active galactic nuclei in pairs show progressively redder rest-frame colours with increasing redshift, particularly at redshifts of $z\gtrsim 0.5$, whereas isolated AGNs and non-AGNs in pairs show no significant colour evolution and remain at $\mathrm{M_g-M_r}\sim0.65$. Pairs hosting AGNs are also preferentially morphologically disturbed interacting systems found at smaller projected separations and velocity offsets, consistent with more dynamically advanced interactions. Conclusions. These results provide evidence of a redshift-dependent link between galaxy interactions and AGN activity, suggesting that interactions play an increasingly important role in triggering nuclear activity at intermediate redshifts. This study highlights the unique capability of PAUS to probe AGN-galaxy interaction connections beyond the local Universe with unprecedented statistical power.

AI.tldr: Using PAUS photometric redshifts, the study links AGN activity to galaxy pairs out to z~1, finding that AGNs in pairs become progressively redder with redshift and preferentially reside in morphologically disturbed, closer interacting systems.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether and how galaxy interactions are connected to AGN activity beyond the local Universe, a regime previously limited by the lack of sufficient redshift coverage and statistical power.
AI.method: Identified 16,824 galaxy pairs (r_p<100 kpc, ΔV<3500 km/s) and cross-matched PAUS galaxies with multi-wavelength AGN catalogues, yielding 270 AGNs in pairs from a parent sample of 8,880 AGNs. Built control samples of isolated AGNs, non-AGNs in pairs, and isolated non-AGNs matched in redshift, absolute magnitude, and environment.
AI.result: AGNs in pairs show progressively redder rest-frame colours with increasing redshift, notably at z≳0.5, while isolated AGNs and non-AGNs in pairs show no significant colour evolution (staying at M_g−M_r~0.65). Pairs hosting AGNs are preferentially morphologically disturbed, with smaller projected separations and velocity offsets, indicating more dynamically advanced interactions.
AI.conclusion: There is a redshift-dependent link between galaxy interactions and AGN activity, suggesting interactions play an increasingly important role in triggering nuclear activity at intermediate redshifts. PAUS enables probing the AGN–interaction connection beyond the local Universe with unprecedented statistical power.

title: Analog Electronic Computation of Stellar Structure: Polytropic Benchmarks, Circuit Scaling, and Error-Controlled Verification
comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables
summary: We present an electronic analog-computing framework for static stellar-structure equations and verify it using polytropic Lane-Emden benchmarks with known or high-accuracy reference solutions. Starting from an exploratory operational-amplifier and multiplier circuit, we identify sign, coefficient, central-regularity, and signal-conditioning problems that complicate direct electronic implementation. We develop dimensionless first-order formulations, derive regular finite-radius initial conditions, and construct voltage-scaled analog architectures with controlled signal headroom. The principal formulation uses a positive derivative state and reproduces the surface locations and dimensionless mass coefficients of the n = 0, 1, and 3 polytropes at the ideal scaled-voltage level. A common circuit architecture accommodates all three benchmarks, while the nonlinear n = 3 case demonstrates how voltage scaling and computation-speed adjustments can preserve the governing equations. Sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations quantify the propagation of calibration uncertainties into stellar observables. A separate regularized n = 1 circuit, implemented using AD734 and OPAx197 vendor macromodels, passes all 67 deterministic certification cases and three independently seeded Monte Carlo populations of 1000 cases each. All cases satisfy the predefined first-zero error tolerance of 0.020, with no saturation or convergence failures. A stricter 0.1% accuracy threshold is reported for characterization but is not used as the certification criterion. We also demonstrate a dimensionless four-state radiative extension beyond polytropic models. The results establish a reproducible framework for analog computation of stellar-structure benchmarks while explicitly distinguishing ideal calculations, vendor-macromodel verification, and future physical-hardware validation.

AI.tldr: An electronic analog-computing framework for static stellar-structure equations is developed and verified against polytropic Lane-Emden benchmarks, using dimensionless first-order formulations, regular finite-radius initial conditions, and voltage-scaled circuits; a regularized n=1 implementation passes all 67 deterministic and 3x1000 Monte Carlo certification cases.
AI.motivation: Direct analog implementation of stellar-structure equations is obstructed by sign, coefficient, central-regularity, and signal-conditioning problems; the paper aims to establish a reproducible, verifiable framework for analog computation of these benchmarks.
AI.method: Dimensionless first-order reformulations with regular finite-radius initial conditions; voltage-scaled operational-amplifier/multiplier architectures with controlled signal headroom; a common circuit for n = 0, 1, 3 polytropes (nonlinear n = 3 handled via voltage scaling and computation-speed adjustment); sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation; a separate regularized n = 1 circuit built on AD734 and OPAx197 vendor macromodels; and a dimensionless four-state radiative extension.
AI.result: The principal formulation reproduces surface locations and dimensionless mass coefficients of the n = 0, 1, 3 polytropes at the ideal scaled-voltage level; the regularized n = 1 circuit passes all 67 deterministic certification cases and three independently seeded Monte Carlo populations of 1000 cases each, all within the 0.020 first-zero error tolerance with no saturation or convergence failures; a stricter 0.1% threshold is reported for characterization only.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a reproducible framework for analog computation of stellar-structure benchmarks, explicitly distinguishing ideal calculations, vendor-macromodel verification, and future physical-hardware validation.

title: Optical-Infrared Extinction Variation in Nearby Molecular Clouds
summary: The dust extinction curve is an important probe of the properties of dust grains, particularly their size distribution. The properties of dust grains are expected to change significantly in dense molecular clouds due to shielding from interstellar radiation and increased frequency of grain-grain and grain-gas collisions. We measure the dust extinction curve shape parameter R(V) in 9 nearby, dense molecular clouds using data from the APOGEE spectroscopic survey, in combination with ten-band photometry from PS1, 2MASS, and WISE. We analyze the results to determine how the extinction curve varies in nearby molecular clouds. We find that most molecular clouds show a positive correlation between R(V) and E(B-V), but the strength of the correlation varies significantly between clouds. In addition, we find that the clouds with the strongest correlation tend to have very high dispersion in R(V) at fixed E(B-V), which tightens dramatically when clouds are subdivided into separate regions. This suggests that local environmental conditions beyond density shape the R(V)-E(B-V) relation.

AI.tldr: Dust extinction curves (parameterized by R(V)) are measured in 9 nearby dense molecular clouds using APOGEE spectroscopy combined with PS1, 2MASS, and WISE photometry, revealing cloud-dependent R(V)–E(B-V) correlations that indicate local environmental conditions shape dust grain properties.
AI.motivation: Dust grain properties, especially their size distribution, are expected to change significantly in dense molecular clouds due to shielding from interstellar radiation and increased grain-grain and grain-gas collisions. The extinction curve shape is a key probe of these changes, but how the curve varies across and within nearby molecular clouds is not well characterized.
AI.method: R(V) is measured in 9 nearby dense molecular clouds using APOGEE spectroscopic survey data combined with ten-band photometry from PS1, 2MASS, and WISE. The resulting R(V) values are analyzed to characterize how the extinction curve varies with cloud environment and E(B-V).
AI.result: Most molecular clouds show a positive correlation between R(V) and E(B-V), but the strength of this correlation varies significantly between clouds. Clouds with the strongest correlation tend to have very high dispersion in R(V) at fixed E(B-V); this dispersion tightens dramatically when clouds are subdivided into separate regions.
AI.conclusion: The R(V)–E(B-V) relation is not uniform across clouds, and the reduction of R(V) dispersion upon subdividing clouds implies that local environmental conditions beyond density shape the R(V)–E(B-V) relation and thus dust grain properties.

title: Charting the Galactic Underworld II: Strategies for Identifying BHs and NSs with LISA
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, submitted to AAS journals - comments welcome!
summary: Stellar-mass black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs) observed by space-based gravitational-wave detectors offer constraints on binary stellar evolution that are complementary to those from ground- based detectors. The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to detect hundreds of double compact objects (DCOs) containing a BH or NS, but distinguishing these sources from the far more numerous double white dwarfs (WDWDs) may prove challenging. We use adaptive importance sampling with COSMIC to synthesise large populations of BHBH, BHNS, NSNS, BHWD, and NSWD binaries. We combine these binaries with a Milky Way star-formation history and integrate their Galactic orbits with cogsworth, repeating our simulations for a grid of variations in uncertain (binary) stellar physics. We find that LISA detections are largely insensitive to the changes in Galactic position resulting from natal kicks. We then assess how well chirp mass, eccentricity, distance from the Galactic plane, and orbital frequency distinguish BH- and NS-hosting DCOs from WDWDs, accounting for LISA measurement uncertainties. Using chirp mass alone distinguishes only 50-60% of BHBHs and BHNSs, and ~40% of NSNSs, but combining this with orbital frequency recovers 90-100% of BHBHs and BHNSs and around ~50% of NSNSs, with eccentricity further improving the recovery of NSNSs to around 60-70%. Distance from the Galactic plane adds little discriminating power, though it can recover a handful of NSWDs that are missed otherwise. These methods will help identify a significantly larger number of BHs and NSs in LISA data that would be missed by a chirp mass cut alone.

AI.tldr: LISA will detect hundreds of BH/NS-hosting double compact objects alongside far more numerous double white dwarfs; the authors show that combining chirp mass with orbital frequency (and eccentricity) recovers up to 90-100% of BH-containing sources that a chirp-mass cut alone would miss.
AI.motivation: Space-based detectors like LISA offer stellar-mass BH and NS constraints complementary to ground-based detectors, but the far more abundant double white dwarfs (WDWDs) may be confused with the rarer BH/NS-hosting DCOs, so a robust discrimination strategy is needed.
AI.method: Adaptive importance sampling with COSMIC synthesizes large populations of BHBH, BHNS, NSNS, BHWD and NSWD binaries; these are combined with a Milky Way star-formation history and integrated in Galactic orbits with cogsworth across a grid of uncertain binary stellar-physics variations. Discrimination among chirp mass, eccentricity, distance from the Galactic plane, and orbital frequency is assessed under LISA measurement uncertainties.
AI.result: LISA detections are largely insensitive to Galactic-position changes from natal kicks. Chirp mass alone distinguishes only 50-60% of BHBHs and BHNSs and ~40% of NSNSs; adding orbital frequency recovers 90-100% of BHBHs and BHNSs and ~50% of NSNSs; adding eccentricity lifts NSNS recovery to ~60-70%. Distance from the Galactic plane adds little, though it recovers a few NSWDs.
AI.conclusion: Multi-parameter discrimination (chirp mass + orbital frequency + eccentricity) identifies significantly more BH and NS sources in LISA data than a chirp-mass cut alone, improving the astrophysical yield of the mission.

title: Optical and near-infrared s-process abundance scales in the Galactic disc
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: A discrepancy has recently emerged between optical and near-infrared (NIR) s-process abundance scales, particularly for Neodymium (Nd). We investigated this issue using a direct cross-match between the optical Gaia-ESO Survey (DR5) and NIR SDSS-V/MWM (DR19). While atmospheric parameters and Cerium (Ce) abundances exhibit robust 1:1 correlations, Nd displays a systematic X-shaped vertical stretching. Our analysis reveals that the SDSS-V pipeline expands intrinsic Nd variations by a scaling factor of 5.54 relative to the stable optical baseline. This phenomenon is driven by baseline compression in the APOGEE H-band, where the growth of the molecular forest (CN and CO) at high metallicities depresses the local continuum. This forces the chi^2 minimisation engine in the NIR abundance determination to inflate derived abundances to reach mathematical convergence. We provide an empirical calibration framework to reconcile these disparate regimes. This correction effectively eliminates the contradictory negative radial [Nd/Fe] gradient of -0.052 dex/kpc reported in recent NIR surveys, bringing them into alignment with the rising trends established by the optical high-resolution Gaia-ESO survey. These results demonstrate that the observed scale expansion is a spectroscopic artefact of line-blanketing rather than a physical Galactic trend.

AI.tldr: A direct optical–NIR cross-match (Gaia-ESO DR5 vs. SDSS-V/MWM DR19) shows Nd abundances from the NIR pipeline are artificially inflated (×5.54) by H-band continuum suppression from CN/CO line blanketing; an empirical calibration removes the spurious negative [Nd/Fe] radial gradient and reconciles NIR with optical trends.
AI.motivation: A discrepancy has emerged between optical and NIR s-process abundance scales, especially for Nd. The authors aim to determine whether the divergent Nd results (including a reported negative radial [Nd/Fe] gradient) reflect a physical Galactic trend or a spectroscopic artefact.
AI.method: Direct star-by-star cross-match between the optical Gaia-ESO Survey (DR5) and NIR SDSS-V/MWM (DR19). They compare atmospheric parameters and Ce (a control s-process element), then quantify the Nd scaling relationship between surveys. They attribute the effect to baseline/continuum compression in the APOGEE H-band caused by growing CN and CO molecular forests at high metallicity, which biases the chi^2-minimisation abundance engine, and then derive an empirical calibration.
AI.result: Atmospheric parameters and Ce abundances show robust 1:1 correlations, but Nd exhibits a systematic X-shaped vertical stretching. The SDSS-V pipeline amplifies intrinsic Nd scatter by a factor of 5.54 relative to the optical baseline. Applying the empirical calibration eliminates the contradictory negative radial [Nd/Fe] gradient of -0.052 dex/kpc from NIR surveys, aligning them with the rising trends of Gaia-ESO.
AI.conclusion: The optical–NIR Nd scale discrepancy is a spectroscopic artefact of H-band line blanketing (continuum suppression driving inflated abundances under chi^2 convergence), not a physical Galactic gradient. The proposed empirical calibration reconciles the two abundance regimes and cautions against interpreting NIR s-process abundance scales without accounting for line-blanketing effects.

title: AGB-star Mass Transfer Products in Stellar Streams as Tracers of Density in Dissolved Star Clusters
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: The least dense globular clusters (GCs) appear to host the highest fractions of stars with chemical signatures of mass transfer from asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companions. Recent observations suggest the fraction may be even higher in stellar streams that are debris of tidally disrupted (preferentially low-density) GCs. We explore whether this is attributable to lower encounter rates in less-dense GCs allowing more of the relevant binaries to survive dynamical hardening, or outright disruption, long enough to undergo AGB mass transfer. We run a small suite of GC simulations varying initial density using the code CMC with its latest observationally motivated binary prescriptions. Using CMC's built-in COSMIC code for binary stellar evolution, we first identify primordial binaries that would, if left unperturbed, likely undergo AGB mass transfer via either standard or wind Roche-lobe overflow. We then check how many of those binaries survive GC dynamics in CMC long enough to experience AGB mass transfer. We find that wind Roche-lobe overflow is necessary to reproduce the fraction of (sub)giant stars in Galactic GCs that are likely products of AGB mass transfer (~1%) and that binary dynamics plausibly explain why this fraction appears lower in dense, intact GCs than stellar streams. The abundance of mass-transfer products (also collision products and binaries) in upcoming surveys of stellar streams without known progenitors will thus probe the densities of dissolved GCs---difficult to determine otherwise but key to improved stream modeling and predicted rates of many astrophysical transients.

AI.tldr: Low-density globular clusters (and their stellar-stream debris) show high fractions of stars chemically polluted by AGB mass transfer because their lower encounter rates preserve the relevant binaries; wind Roche-lobe overflow is required to match the observed ~1% mass-transfer-product fraction.
AI.motivation: Observations indicate that the least dense GCs host the highest fractions of stars bearing chemical signatures of AGB mass transfer, and the fraction appears even higher in stellar streams that are debris of tidally disrupted, preferentially low-density GCs. The authors ask whether this trend is explained by lower stellar encounter rates in less-dense GCs, which would let the relevant binaries avoid dynamical hardening or disruption long enough to undergo AGB mass transfer.
AI.method: A small suite of globular-cluster simulations with CMC, varying initial density and using the latest observationally motivated binary prescriptions. The built-in COSMIC binary stellar-evolution code is used to first identify primordial binaries that would, if unperturbed, likely undergo AGB mass transfer via either standard Roche-lobe overflow or wind Roche-lobe overflow; the simulations then track how many of these binaries survive cluster dynamics long enough to actually experience AGB mass transfer.
AI.result: Wind Roche-lobe overflow is necessary to reproduce the ~1% fraction of (sub)giant stars in Galactic GCs that are likely products of AGB mass transfer. Binary dynamics plausibly explain why this fraction is lower in dense, intact GCs than in stellar streams.
AI.conclusion: The abundance of mass-transfer products (alongside collision products and binaries) in upcoming surveys of stellar streams with unknown progenitors can probe the densities of dissolved GCs—otherwise difficult to determine but essential for improved stream modeling and predicted rates of many astrophysical transients.

title: JWST observations of the planetary nebula NGC 6302 IV: PAH spectral characteristics, formation and evolution
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables including 6 in appendices, accepted in MNRAS
summary: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and carbonaceous dust have been observed in Oxygen-rich planetary nebulae (PNe), yet their formation and evolution in these environments is an open question. We aim to study the formation and evolution of the PAHs in the O-rich PN NGC 6302, by characterizing the PAH emission throughout this object. We obtained JWST MIRI IFU spectroscopic observations of NGC 6302 pointed at its central source. From these, we extract four template spectra that are representative of the variation in PAH emission throughout NGC 6302. We detect the major PAH features at 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.2, and 12.7 $μ$m, and several minor PAH features. The template spectra vary in terms of their PAH feature widths, peak wavelengths, and relative intensities. The 11.2 $μ$m PAH feature is class B, typical for PNe. The 6-9 $μ$m PAH features are class A, which is less common for PNe. We estimate the PAH charge to be 75% cations on average, based on the 7.7/11.2 PAH feature ratio. The relative strengths of the 11-15 $μ$m PAH features indicate a range of PAH edge structures. To ensure consistency in our observations and explain variable PAH feature widths, we propose a variation in the size of the PAHs throughout NGC 6302, and suggest variation in the shielding of these PAHs. The PAHs range from large and non-compact, to small and compact. We find that NGC 6302 formed PAHs in-situ in the current PN phase, likely from small hydrocarbons formed by the photodissociation of CO.

AI.tldr: JWST MIRI IFU spectroscopy of the O-rich planetary nebula NGC 6302 reveals spatially variable PAH emission, indicating in-situ PAH formation during the current PN phase.
AI.motivation: PAHs and carbonaceous dust are observed in oxygen-rich planetary nebulae, but their formation and evolution in such environments remains an open question. The authors aim to characterize PAH emission throughout the O-rich PN NGC 6302 to understand how these molecules form and evolve.
AI.method: JWST MIRI IFU spectroscopic observations of NGC 6302 centered on its central source. Four representative template spectra are extracted to capture the spatial variation of PAH emission. The major PAH features at 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.2, and 12.7 μm and several minor features are analyzed for width, peak wavelength, and relative intensity. PAH charge is estimated from the 7.7/11.2 feature ratio; edge structures are inferred from the 11–15 μm features.
AI.result: Template spectra show variation in PAH feature widths, peak wavelengths, and relative intensities. The 11.2 μm feature is class B (typical for PNe), while the 6–9 μm features are class A (less common). PAH charge is ~75% cations on average. The 11–15 μm features indicate a range of PAH edge structures. The variability is explained by a range of PAH sizes (large/non-compact to small/compact) and varying shielding.
AI.conclusion: NGC 6302 formed PAHs in-situ during the current PN phase, likely from small hydrocarbons produced by photodissociation of CO.

title: Solar Photospheric Flows and the Origin of Active Regions
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures
summary: The early evolutionary stages of some active regions (ARs) are analysed with the aim of resolving one of the paramount-importance problems of heliophysics: what plays a primary, active role in the formation of active regions and sunspots---magnetic fields or motion of solar plasma? In particular, the first view underlies the popular model of rising $Ω$-shaped, twisted flux-tube loop of strong magnetic field. In this study, optical images obtained by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) of the Solar Dynamics Observatory are used along with full-vector maps of magnetic field based on HMI data. Maps of fluid-particle tracks are constructed using local correlation tracking of photospheric brightness elements. Comparisons of optical and magnetic maps for three developing active regions confirm the conclusion made by Bumba and Howard in the mid-1960s that the supergranulation pattern is not destroyed by the emerging magnetic field of the developing AR, which would be inevitable if a loop of the strong-magnetic-field flux tube rose through the subphotospheric layers. There are no signs of spreading flows on scales comparable to the size of the whole active region. Various forms of dissymmetry between the leading and trailing parts of ARs are revealed. Next, an example of a well-developed sunspot group is considered, which demonstrates that the twist of the magnetic configuration may develop much later than the group starts growing. It is concluded that plasma flows appear to be determinant with respect to magnetic fields. The considered scenarios of the origin of ARs are in sharp contradiction with the rising-tube model.

AI.tldr: Analysis of early-stage active regions using HMI optical and vector-magnetogram data plus local correlation tracking shows supergranulation persists undisturbed through flux emergence, contradicting the rising twisted flux-tube model and indicating plasma flows drive magnetic structure.
AI.motivation: To resolve a fundamental heliophysics question: whether magnetic fields or plasma motions play the primary, active role in forming active regions (ARs) and sunspots—specifically testing the popular rising Ω-shaped twisted flux-tube loop model against the alternative that flows are determinant.
AI.method: Optical images and full-vector magnetic field maps from SDO/HMI are compared for developing ARs; fluid-particle track maps are derived via local correlation tracking (LCT) of photospheric brightness elements to characterize supergranulation and flow patterns.
AI.result: For three developing ARs, supergranulation is not destroyed by emerging flux (confirming Bumba & Howard 1965), no spreading flows on AR-wide scales are found, and various leading–trailing asymmetries appear. In a well-developed sunspot group, magnetic twist develops much later than group growth begins.
AI.conclusion: Plasma flows appear determinant with respect to magnetic fields; the observed AR formation scenarios sharply contradict the rising-tube model.

title: A Potential New Dimension of Astrophysical Aromatic Functionalization: Phosphaethynyl (CP) Derivatives
summary: Quantum chemical computations outline a thermodynamically viable, low-temperature, gas-phase formation pathway for phosphaethynyl cyclopropenylidene ($c$-C$_3$HCP), resulting from cyclopropenylidene ($c$-C$_3$H$_2$) and the phosphaethynyl (CP) radical. Given the detections of both $c$-C$_3$H$_2$ and the CP radical toward circumstellar shells along with the provided reaction pathway, $c$-C$_3$HCP is a potentially present astro-molecule which could be searched for in phosphorus rich environments. The reaction of CP and benzene (C$_6$H$_6$) to produce phosphaethynyl benzene (C$_6$H$_5$CP) is also explored. A marginally emerged, but tentative, transition state is identified for this reaction using certain quantum chemical approaches but not others. Consequently, the formation of CP-substituted benzoid polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in astrophysical environments from CP + PAH reactions is possible but currently uncertain. Additionally, explicitly correlated coupled cluster quartic force field and second-order vibrational perturbation theory rovibrational analysis of the vibrational frequencies and rotational constants of $c$-C$_3$HCP are provided, as well as density functional theory predictions of the same for CP-benzene (C$_6$H$_5$CP) and both isomers of CP-naphthalene (C$_1$$_0$H$_7$CP). Our results suggest that IR searches for these molecules would likely be unsuccessful due to the low intensities and coincidence with PAH features, but their large dipole moments could make them feasible to detect with radio astronomy. The barrierless formation of $c$-C$_3$HCP and possibly barrierless synthesis of C$_6$H$_5$CP stand as examples for future investigations of other CP-substituted aromatic molecules, marking the potential beginning of a new frontier of astronomical aromatic functionalization.

AI.tldr: Quantum chemical computations identify a thermodynamically viable, low-temperature, gas-phase route to phosphaethynyl cyclopropenylidene (c-C3HCP) via c-C3H2 + CP radical, assess CP + benzene → C6H5CP, and provide rovibrational data (frequencies, rotational constants) suggesting radio rather than IR detectability.
AI.motivation: Both c-C3H2 and the CP radical have been detected toward circumstellar shells, motivating the question of whether they react to form a phosphorus-bearing astromolecule (c-C3HCP) and whether CP can functionalize aromatic species such as benzene and PAHs, opening a frontier of astronomical aromatic functionalization.
AI.method: Quantum chemical reaction-pathway computations for c-C3H2 + CP and CP + C6H6; identification of a tentative transition state for CP + benzene that appears with some quantum chemical approaches but not others; explicitly correlated coupled cluster quartic force field with second-order vibrational perturbation theory (VPT2) for rovibrational analysis of c-C3HCP; DFT predictions of vibrational frequencies and rotational constants for C6H5CP and both isomers of C10H7CP.
AI.result: The c-C3HCP formation pathway is thermodynamically viable at low temperature and barrierless, making c-C3HCP a plausible target in phosphorus-rich environments. The CP + benzene transition state is only marginally found and method-dependent, so CP-substituted benzoid PAH formation is possible but currently uncertain. IR searches are likely unsuccessful due to low intensities and overlap with PAH features, whereas the large dipole moments make radio detection feasible for c-C3HCP, C6H5CP, and CP-naphthalene isomers.
AI.conclusion: Barrierless synthesis of c-C3HCP and possibly of C6H5CP exemplify CP-substituted aromatic chemistry, providing templates for future studies of related molecules and marking a potential new frontier of astronomical aromatic functionalization; radio astronomy is the recommended detection strategy.

title: Detection of Solar-like Oscillations and Granulation at Infrared Wavelengths using JWST
comment: Recently resubmitted to APJLetters following favourable referee report
summary: Stellar oscillations and granulation are key probes of stellar convection, one of the most poorly understood processes in stars. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation, but hitherto both processes have only been measured at optical wavelengths. Here we present the first detection of oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 that were obtained to study the atmosphere of an exoplanet. We find that the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but with a functional form that deviates from simple blackbody scaling. The detection opens the door to detailed tests of 3D convection models, facilitates the combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands for exoplanet observations, and supports the predicted asteroseismic yields from the infrared time-domain data that will soon be obtained by the Roman Space Telescope.

AI.tldr: First detection of stellar oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths using JWST time-series of the F6V star WASP-121; amplitudes decrease with wavelength as expected but deviate from simple blackbody scaling.
AI.motivation: Stellar oscillations and granulation probe convection, a poorly understood process. Models predict strong wavelength dependence of their amplitudes, yet both had only been measured at optical wavelengths, leaving the infrared regime untested.
AI.method: Analysis of JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 (originally obtained to study an exoplanet atmosphere), measuring oscillation and granulation amplitudes at infrared wavelengths and comparing them with models and blackbody scaling.
AI.result: Oscillation and granulation amplitudes decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but the functional form deviates from simple blackbody scaling.
AI.conclusion: The detection enables detailed tests of 3D convection models, combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands, and supports predicted asteroseismic yields from upcoming Roman Space Telescope infrared time-domain data.

title: Rest-frame Ultraviolet Variability of Quasars in the Cosmic Himalayas Overdensity
summary: Some high-redshift overdensities show an enhanced incidence of AGNs, suggesting that large-scale environment may influence supermassive black hole fuelling and triggering. Whether environment also affects AGN variability remains unclear.Using the Cosmic Himalayas (CH), an extreme concentration of 11 type 1 quasars at z=2.16-2.20, we investigate possible offsets in rest-frame ultraviolet variability relative to quasars with comparable redshifts, black hole masses, and Eddington ratios.We construct a parent sample of 1,138 Stripe 82 quasars at 2.11<=z<=2.25 and combine photometry from the SDSS, the PS1, and the ZTF to build observer-frame g- and r-band light curves spanning up to 27~yr. We compare DRW parameters and ensemble structure functions (SFs) with control pseudo-samples matched in black hole mass and Eddington ratio, and use injection--recovery simulations to forecast the detectability of a CH-like offset.The CH quasars show a tendency toward shorter DRW damping timescales (median offsets of -0.32 and -0.13 dex in g and r) and slightly higher asymptotic amplitudes. None of the four DRW comparisons is statistically significant, including the largest offset in the g-band damping timescale (p=0.16). Ensemble SFs generally exceed matched-control medians, although 18 of 19 lag bins per band remain within the 95% pointwise envelopes. Assuming a true uniform -0.32 dex g-band timescale offset, injection--recovery simulations predict an 80% probability of nominal 3sigma detection with approximately 60 quasars of comparable variability scatter and data quality.If confirmed, the tentative variability offsets may suggest that large-scale environment influences accretion-flow variability beyond its potential role in quasar triggering. Larger samples with higher-precision light curves, such as those expected from the LSST, are required to test this possibility.

AI.tldr: Using 11 quasars in the z≈2.2 "Cosmic Himalayas" overdensity, the authors search for rest-frame UV variability offsets relative to matched Stripe 82 quasars; offsets are tentative (shorter DRW damping timescales, mildly elevated structure functions) but not statistically significant, and LSST-scale samples are needed.
AI.motivation: High-redshift overdensities show enhanced AGN incidence, hinting that large-scale environment influences black hole fuelling; whether environment also modulates AGN variability is unknown.
AI.method: Combine SDSS, PS1 and ZTF photometry for 1,138 Stripe 82 quasars at 2.11≤z≤2.25 to build up to 27-yr observer-frame g- and r-band light curves. Compare DRW parameters and ensemble structure functions of the Cosmic Himalayas quasars against pseudo-samples matched in black hole mass and Eddington ratio, and run injection–recovery simulations to forecast detectability.
AI.result: CH quasars show shorter DRW damping timescales (median −0.32 dex in g, −0.13 dex in r) and slightly higher asymptotic amplitudes, but none of the four DRW comparisons is significant (largest: g-band timescale, p=0.16). Ensemble SFs exceed matched-control medians, yet 18 of 19 lag bins per band lie within 95% pointwise envelopes. Simulations predict 80% power for a nominal 3σ detection of a true −0.32 dex offset with ~60 quasars of comparable quality.
AI.conclusion: Tentative variability offsets, if confirmed, would suggest environment affects accretion-flow variability beyond quasar triggering; larger, higher-precision light curves (e.g., LSST) are required.

title: Distinct stellar-parameter dependencies of granulation and mesogranulation in red giants
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables, including appendix. Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Granulation and mesogranulation represent different spatial and temporal scales of convection, but are commonly assumed to follow the same stellar atmospheric scaling relations in red giants. We test this assumption using the largest sample assembled for this purpose to date -- 9,328 Kepler red giants spanning the red giant branch and red clump phase, cross-matched with APOGEE stellar parameters. We model each star's power spectrum background to obtain the radius-corrected amplitude and characteristic frequency of both components, and derive empirical scaling relations with effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity through Bayesian model comparison. Gaussian Process and symbolic regression provide independent validation. We find that granulation and mesogranulation are not self-similar: their surface-gravity dependencies are statistically indistinguishable, consistent with a shared envelope geometry, but their temperature dependencies diverge: mesogranulation's amplitude rises steeply with Teff, whereas granulation's shows no statistically justified dependence, and both frequencies respond weakly and similarly. We propose that this pattern is consistent with granulation forming in a thin near-surface layer, where radiation takes over from convection and the Mach number depends only weakly on Teff. Mesogranulation originates deeper, where convection carries the full flux and its Mach number and cell size increase with Teff. Metallicity raises both amplitudes but has little effect on the frequencies. Our results indicate that the self-similarity assumption underlying two-component background models does not hold, with direct implications for background modeling and its downstream application in Galactic archaeology.

AI.tldr: Granulation and mesogranulation in red giants are not self-similar: their surface-gravity scalings match, but their temperature scalings diverge, invalidating the self-similarity assumption behind two-component background models.
AI.motivation: Two-component background models of red-giant power spectra commonly assume granulation and mesogranulation follow the same stellar-atmospheric scaling relations, despite representing different spatial and temporal convection scales; this assumption had not been tested on a large sample.
AI.method: The authors assembled 9,328 Kepler red giants (RGB and red clump) cross-matched with APOGEE parameters, modelled each star's power-spectrum background to extract radius-corrected amplitudes and characteristic frequencies for both components, and derived empirical scaling relations with Teff, log g, and metallicity via Bayesian model comparison, validating independently with Gaussian Processes and symbolic regression.
AI.result: Surface-gravity dependencies of the two components are statistically indistinguishable (consistent with shared envelope geometry), but temperature dependencies diverge: mesogranulation amplitude rises steeply with Teff while granulation shows no justified Teff dependence; both frequencies respond weakly and similarly. Metallicity raises both amplitudes with little effect on frequencies.
AI.conclusion: The self-similarity assumption underlying two-component background models does not hold. The pattern is interpreted as granulation forming in a thin near-surface layer (radiation-dominated, weakly Teff-dependent Mach number) and mesogranulation originating deeper where convection carries the full flux, with Mach number and cell size increasing with Teff; this has direct implications for background modelling and downstream Galactic archaeology applications.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. II. The Multi-component Age-Metallicity Structure of the High-$α$ Disk
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Whether the high-$α$ disk experienced a continuous or episodic star-formation history remains an open question. Here we investigate the age--metallicity distribution of the high-$α$ disk using approximately 145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants with $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]>-1$, 6.5~kpc $\lesssim R\lesssim9.5$~kpc, and $|Z|\lesssim1.5$~kpc. We adopt a forward-modelling framework that accounts for individual age and metallicity uncertainties and corrects for sample selection effects. The reconstructed distribution reveals two components: a broad, dominant population peaking at $\sim10.6$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.38$, and an older, more metal-poor population peaking at $\sim12.4$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.79$. These features suggest an episodic history of star formation and chemical enrichment in the high-$α$ disk, qualitatively consistent with cosmological simulations in which recurrent gas accretion drives variations in the star formation rate. The age of the older component is close to the $\sim12.3$~Gyr epoch inferred for the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles accretion event, suggesting a possible connection between this early interaction and enhanced disk star formation. There is tentative evidence that the dominant population is possibly composed of two sub-components with age distributions peaking at $\sim11.1$ Gyr and $\sim10.0$ Gyr, respectively. Together, these results favour a picture in which the high-$α$ disk was built through recurrent episodes of enhanced star formation rather than a single temporally smooth phase, even for the regime of ${\rm [Fe/H]}>-1$.

AI.tldr: Using ~145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants, the high-α disk's age–metallicity distribution is reconstructed via forward modelling, revealing two distinct components (~10.6 Gyr, [Fe/H]≈−0.38; ~12.4 Gyr, [Fe/H]≈−0.79) that indicate an episodic rather than continuous star-formation history.
AI.motivation: It remains unresolved whether the high-α disk formed through continuous or episodic star formation. Clarifying this requires a robust, selection-corrected age–metallicity distribution over a large, well-defined sample.
AI.method: A forward-modelling framework is applied to ~145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants with [Fe/H]>−1, 6.5 ≲ R ≲ 9.5 kpc, and |Z| ≲ 1.5 kpc. The model incorporates individual age and metallicity uncertainties and corrects for sample selection effects to reconstruct the underlying age–metallicity distribution.
AI.result: The reconstructed distribution shows a dominant broad population peaking at ~10.6 Gyr with [Fe/H]≈−0.38, plus an older, more metal-poor component at ~12.4 Gyr with [Fe/H]≈−0.79. The older component's age aligns with the ~12.3 Gyr epoch proposed for the Low-energy–Kraken–Heracles accretion event. Tentative evidence suggests the dominant population may split into sub-components peaking at ~11.1 and ~10.0 Gyr.
AI.conclusion: The high-α disk experienced episodic star formation and chemical enrichment, qualitatively consistent with cosmological simulations where recurrent gas accretion modulates the star-formation rate. The results favour recurrent, punctuated build-up over a single smooth phase, possibly linked to early accretion events, even in the [Fe/H]>−1 regime.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS survey: A Keplerian Circumbinary Disk Candidate in the High-mass Star-forming Region IRAS 08303-4303
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present the ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations of IRAS 08303-4303, a high-mass star-forming region, with an angular resolution of $\sim 0.3''$ ($\sim 700$ au at the distance of 2.35 kpc). Six dense condensations are identified in the 1.3 mm continuum, and at least four of them are associated with molecular outflows. The estimated outflow parameters, particularly mass outflow rates $\geq 10^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, suggest that the driving sources are high-mass young stellar objects. Two of the condensations are forming a wide protobinary system with a separation of $\sim 900$ au. They reside within a single rotating structure, identified as a circumbinary disk which has a mass of about 2 $M_{\odot}$. This structure is traced by multiple molecular lines and exhibits a Keplerian rotation pattern. Based on the Keplerian rotation assumption, the enclosed mass is derived to be between 32 and 61 $M_{\odot}$: 22-43 $M_{\odot}$ for the primary and 10-18 $M_{\odot}$ for the secondary. The circumbinary disk is on the whole gravitationally stable, yet some parts with Toomre $Q < 2$ indicate potential fragmentation. Various molecular lines reveal a streamer-like structure connecting to the circumbinary disk, suggesting transfer of material from the envelope to the protobinary system through it. Despite the observational rarity of such circumbinary disks around high-mass YSOs, the high binary fraction among massive stars underscores their significance. This source, therefore, serves as a key laboratory for understanding the formation of high-mass binary systems.

AI.tldr: ALMA Band 6 observations of IRAS 08303-4303 reveal six dense condensations, at least four driving molecular outflows, and a massive circumbinary disk (~2 Msun) hosting a wide (~900 au) high-mass protobinary with Keplerian rotation and a streamer feeding the system.
AI.motivation: Circumbinary disks around high-mass young stellar objects are observationally rare, yet the high binary fraction among massive stars makes them important for understanding high-mass binary formation. IRAS 08303-4303 is studied as a key laboratory for this process.
AI.method: ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations of IRAS 08303-4303 at ~0.3'' (~700 au) resolution; identification of dense condensations, outflow parameter estimation, multiple molecular line tracing of the circumbinary disk and streamer, and Keplerian rotation modeling to derive enclosed masses and Toomre Q stability analysis.
AI.result: Six dense condensations detected in 1.3 mm continuum, at least four with molecular outflows; outflow rates ≥1e-4 Msun/yr indicate high-mass YSOs. Two condensations form a ~900 au protobinary within a single ~2 Msun Keplerian-rotating circumbinary disk. Enclosed mass is 32-61 Msun (primary 22-43, secondary 10-18). The disk is globally gravitationally stable but locally has Toomre Q < 2 indicating potential fragmentation. A streamer-like structure connecting envelope to disk is traced.
AI.conclusion: IRAS 08303-4303 hosts a rare circumbinary disk around a high-mass protobinary, with envelope material fed via a streamer and possible local fragmentation, serving as a key laboratory for high-mass binary formation.

title: A 13 Year Black Hole Microlensing Survey in Omega Centauri
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Star clusters are born with massive stars that leave behind a large population of stellar mass black holes. These black holes may account for a large fraction of binary black hole mergers seen in gravitational waves as the dense environment enables retention of black holes and the formation of binaries. However, direct measurements of stellar mass black holes in globular clusters are limited, with just a few found in binary systems thus far. In this paper, we examine the possibility of detecting black holes through microlensing in the Milky Way's most massive star cluster, Omega Centauri. We take advantage of a unique dataset of nearly 200 single-band images taken over 13 years with the Hubble Space Telescope to look for the $\sim$1 year long events expected from microlensing of cluster stars by stellar mass black holes. We develop a novel cost function to fit the lensing signatures that we verify using synthetic events, quantifying our completeness. These synthetic events are based on a recent Monte Carlo simulation of Omega Centauri. We also use these synthetic events to train a neural network to most efficiently distinguish observed lensing events. Application of this algorithm to our observed data, and subsequent visual follow-up, show no convincing candidate black hole lensing events. Based on analysis of the simulation data and our completeness, we find that no events would be expected in the data contrary to the expectations from earlier work. We release the photometric dataset used in this work for future use.

AI.tldr: A search for stellar-mass black holes via microlensing of cluster stars in Omega Centauri using 13 years of Hubble Space Telescope imaging, with a novel cost-function and neural-network pipeline, finds no convincing candidate events, consistent with revised simulation-based expectations.
AI.motivation: Stellar-mass black holes are expected to be abundant in massive star clusters and may drive a large fraction of observed binary black hole mergers, yet direct detections in globular clusters remain scarce (only a few in binaries). The dense cluster environment makes microlensing a promising probe, motivating a systematic search in Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's most massive cluster.
AI.method: The authors use a unique dataset of nearly 200 single-band Hubble Space Telescope images spanning 13 years to search for ~1-year-long microlensing events from black holes lensing cluster stars. They develop a novel cost function to fit the lensing signatures, validated and characterized for completeness using synthetic events generated from a recent Monte Carlo simulation of Omega Centauri, and train a neural network on these synthetic events to efficiently identify observed lensing candidates, followed by visual follow-up.
AI.result: Application of the algorithm to the observed data, plus visual follow-up, yields no convincing candidate black hole lensing events. Analysis of simulated data and the measured completeness indicates that no events would be expected in the dataset, contradicting expectations from earlier work.
AI.conclusion: The search finds no black hole microlensing candidates in Omega Centauri, and revised simulation-based completeness shows this null result is consistent with predictions, rather than indicating an absence of black holes; the photometric dataset is released for future use.

title: A precise TESS ephemeris for the short-period binary TIC-259864042
comment: 9 pages, 4 Tables, 9 figures
summary: This paper presents a precise eclipse-timing analysis of TIC 259864042 (= EC 02406--6408, Gaia DR3 4647004122914240640) using eleven sectors of TESS photometry spanning 2018--2025 (7.1 yr). The system exhibits a single deep eclipse with a V-shaped profile at phase 0 and no detectable counterpart at phase 0.5. Four independent period-search methods converge to a common period agreeing to within 7 parts per million. An independent reduction with the SHERLOCK pipeline, using its own 120-second TESS photometry, confirms the same period at the same precision. A joint linear ephemeris fit gives P = 0.46048676 $\pm$ 0.0000001 d (11.059 h) and T_0 = 2458325.70381 $\pm$ 0.00002 BJD, with a residual RMS of 0.87 min across the 7.1-yr baseline. Per-sector ephemeris fits show residual medians within $\pm$0.42 min of zero, confirming that no cycle slip has occurred across the large TESS data gaps. The period is stable at the level of $Δ$BIC = +5.21 (in favour of the constant-period model); an upper limit of $|\dot{P}| \le 1 \times 10^{-9}$ d d$^{-1}$ is placed on any secular period change. A PHOEBE 2.4 fit to the Sector 27 light curve yields $i = 80.8^{\circ} \pm 0.5^{\circ}$, $R_1 = 0.21 \pm 0.01\ R_{\odot}$, $R_2 = 0.25 \pm 0.02\ R_{\odot}$, $q = 0.49 \pm 0.07$, consistent with a grazing detached geometry and a mid-M-dwarf companion. The TESS light curve alone cannot distinguish between the two temperatures 25100 K and 31000 K. The paper discusses the system in the context of the sdB eclipsing binary population, and notes that while the current data are consistent with a short-period sdB+M-dwarf architecture, a phase-resolved spectrum is needed to independently confirm the sdB identification.

AI.tldr: Precise TESS eclipse-timing of TIC 259864042 confirms a stable P = 0.46048676 d period over 7.1 yr, consistent with a grazing short-period sdB+M-dwarf geometry, though the sdB identification needs spectroscopic confirmation.
AI.motivation: The object TIC 259864042 shows a single deep V-shaped eclipse with no secondary eclipse, suggesting a possible short-period sdB eclipsing binary. Establishing a precise, stable ephemeris and characterizing the geometry is needed to place it in the sdB+M-dwarf population.
AI.method: Eleven TESS sectors (2018-2025, 7.1 yr) analysed with eclipse-timing; four independent period-search methods cross-checked; independent SHERLOCK reduction with 120-s photometry; joint linear ephemeris fit plus per-sector fits; BIC-based test of constant vs. changing period; PHOEBE 2.4 modeling of the Sector 27 light curve.
AI.result: Periods agree to 7 ppm across methods; P = 0.46048676 +/- 0.0000001 d (11.059 h), T0 = 2458325.70381 +/- 0.00002 BJD, residual RMS 0.87 min, per-sector residual medians within +/-0.42 min; Delta BIC = +5.21 favoring constant period, |P_dot| <= 1e-9 d/d; PHOEBE gives i = 80.8 +/- 0.5 deg, R1 = 0.21 +/- 0.01 Rsun, R2 = 0.25 +/- 0.02 Rsun, q = 0.49 +/- 0.07 (grazing detached, mid-M companion); photometry alone cannot distinguish 25100 K vs 31000 K.
AI.conclusion: The current data are consistent with a short-period sdB+M-dwarf architecture with a stable period; definitive sdB classification requires a phase-resolved spectrum.

title: Lomb-Scargle Recovery of Periodic Binary Signals across Black Hole Mass and Cadence
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables
summary: Searches for periodic supermassive black hole binaries in quasar light curves rely on recovery fractions, the share of injected signals detected, which forecasts use as detection efficiencies. Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026) measured them for the Lomb-Scargle periodogram on damped-random-walk light curves matched to 12,400 bright, high-mass Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) quasars with Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (DR7) masses. To test them over four decades of mass, we inject their sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of mergers in the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, with magnitudes drawn from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). We apply their threshold in each frequency bin, set by $10^5$ noise-only light curves per binary, on observed PTF cadences, one Stripe 82 cadence and an LSST-like cadence (Legacy Survey of Space and Time). At fixed absolute magnitude $M_i=-23$, sinusoid recovery falls toward high mass, and with DR7 magnitudes it climbs above about $10^8\,M_\odot$, so the magnitude assignment sets the sign of the trend. Above $10^8\,M_\odot$, where their sample lies, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 against their 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, about three times their 22.6 per cent, for reasons mostly unidentified. Denser sampling of the same PTF baselines did not lower recovery in any test. Even at LSST-like cadence we miss most sawtooth signals above $10^8\,M_\odot$. We tabulate recovery per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence, with low-mass values likely too high for a deeper survey.

AI.tldr: Recovery fractions for periodic supermassive black hole binaries are re-derived by injecting sinusoid and sawtooth signals into TNG100-1 merger light curves across four decades of mass; trends depend on magnitude assignment, and LSST-like cadence roughly triples sinusoid recovery while most high-mass sawtooth signals remain undetected.
AI.motivation: Forecast detection efficiencies for periodic SMBH binaries in quasar light curves rest on recovery fractions measured by Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026), but those were derived from a narrow bright, high-mass PTF sample (12,400 quasars), so their validity across four decades of black hole mass and for other cadences is untested.
AI.method: The authors inject the same sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of SMBH mergers from the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, assigning magnitudes from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). Detection thresholds are set per frequency bin from 10^5 noise-only light curves per binary, applied on observed PTF cadences, a Stripe 82 cadence, and an LSST-like cadence.
AI.result: At fixed M_i = -23, sinusoid recovery declines toward high mass, whereas with DR7 magnitudes it rises above ~10^8 M_sun, so the magnitude assignment determines the sign of the trend. Above 10^8 M_sun, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 per cent versus the original 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, roughly three times the original 22.6 per cent, for largely unidentified reasons. Denser sampling of identical PTF baselines never reduced recovery, and most sawtooth signals above 10^8 M_sun are missed even with LSST-like cadence.
AI.conclusion: Recovery fractions are tabulated per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence; low-mass values are likely overoptimistic for a deeper survey, and the strong sensitivity to magnitude assignment and cadence cautions against transferring published detection efficiencies to new survey regimes without re-derivation.

title: Eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We have identified numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triple star systems from observations made with the space telescope TESS. For many of these systems we can potentially determine their dynamical and astrophysical parameters with high precision, in some cases even without the use of radial velocity data. In the present paper we report the comprehensive study of eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems, taken from this larger sample: TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, 385933895. Besides the photometric data from the TESS observations, we obtained supplementary ground-based photometric measurements, as well as radial velocity measurements for some of the systems. The eclipse timing variation curves extracted from the TESS data and from the ground-based follow up data, the photometric light curves, radial velocity data, and the spectral energy distribution are combined in a complex photodynamical analysis to yield the stellar and orbital parameters for all of the investigated systems. The outer periods are in the range of 63-294 days, including the currently sixth tightest known triple system, TI 385933895 with an outer to inner period ratio of 9.82. We find that all of the triples are nearly coplanar, with mutual inclination angles of <=2.5deg. Despite such flatness, we still detect eclipse depth variations in TIC 220456364 that are induced by orbital plane precession. Moreover, we find that TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple system. Finally we make some statistical assessments of a number of the orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances of these systems.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive photodynamical study of eight new TESS triply eclipsing hierarchical triple systems (some possibly quadruple), deriving precise stellar and orbital parameters and reporting near-coplanar configurations and precession-driven eclipse depth variations.
AI.motivation: Numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triples have been found with TESS, and such systems offer the potential to determine dynamical and astrophysical parameters at high precision—sometimes even without radial velocity data. A detailed characterization of newly identified systems is needed.
AI.method: Combined TESS photometry, ground-based follow-up photometry, radial velocity measurements (for some systems), eclipse timing variation curves, light curves, and spectral energy distributions in a complex photodynamical analysis to derive stellar and orbital parameters for TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, and 385933895.
AI.result: Outer periods span 63–294 days; TIC 385933895 is the sixth tightest known triple with an outer-to-inner period ratio of 9.82. All triples are nearly coplanar (mutual inclinations ≤2.5°). Eclipse depth variations induced by orbital plane precession are detected in TIC 220456364, and TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple. Statistical assessments of orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances are provided.
AI.conclusion: The eight systems are well-characterized triply eclipsing triples with precise parameters; the near-coplanarity does not preclude observable precession-driven eclipse depth changes, and at least one system is a hierarchical quadruple. These results inform the broader TESS triple population statistically.
