title: A recurring changing state AGN discovered in the SAMI Galaxy Survey and SDSS
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in PASA
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the AGN in galaxy J085337.26+014303.6 at z=0.0582. A combination of SDSS and SAMI Galaxy Survey data shows that this object has gone through at least one full changing-look AGN cycle, from type 1.9 in 2001 to type 1 in 2015 and 2021, and then type 1.9 again in 2022. While the broad lines in this object show evidence of dust obscuration, detailed spectral analysis plus WISE photometry demonstrate that the changes in this object are related to a physical state change, not changing obscuration. In fact, the WISE light curve suggests that this object may have briefly returned to a type 1.9 state in 2020. In the optical, the host galaxy dominates the light (e.g. only ~10 per cent contribution from the AGN at 4000 Angstoms within a central aperture), even in the high state. In contrast, the brightest WISE W2-band measurements place the AGN at a similar luminosity to the entire host galaxy. The broad Balmer lines show evidence of multiple components, with a weak very-broad component (FWHM=5000-6000 km/s) visible in the low type 1.9 state, and a stronger broad component of FWHM~2000 km/s dominating in the high type 1 state. We propose that this is caused by two spatially distinct regions within the broad line region.

AI.tldr: A detailed multi-epoch study of J085337.26+014303.6 (z=0.0582) reveals at least one full changing-look AGN (CL-AGN) cycle (type 1.9 → 1 → 1.9), driven by a physical state change rather than variable obscuration, with two kinematically distinct broad-line regions.
AI.motivation: Changing-look AGN offer a rare probe of AGN accretion-state transitions, yet the origin of the type transitions (intrinsic physical change vs. variable dust obscuration) and the structure of the broad line region (BLR) during these events remain debated. The authors aim to discriminate between these scenarios for a single well-sampled object.
AI.method: Combined SDSS and SAMI Galaxy Survey optical spectroscopy spanning 2001–2022, plus WISE mid-infrared photometry/light curve. Spectral analysis (broad Balmer line decomposition, host-galaxy subtraction) and WISE photometry are used to test obscuration vs. intrinsic-change interpretations and to characterize BLR components.
AI.result: The object cycles from type 1.9 (2001) to type 1 (2015, 2021) and back to type 1.9 (2022), with WISE data hinting at a brief return to type 1.9 in 2020. Dust obscuration is present in the broad lines but does not explain the transitions. The host galaxy dominates optical light (~10% AGN contribution at 4000 Å in a central aperture even in the high state), whereas the brightest WISE W2 measurements place the AGN at a luminosity comparable to the whole host. Broad Balmer lines show two components: a weak very-broad component (FWHM 5000–6000 km/s) visible in the low state, and a stronger broad component (FWHM ~2000 km/s) dominating the high state.
AI.conclusion: The CL transitions in J085337.26+014303.6 are intrinsic (physical state changes), not obscuration-driven, and the multi-component Balmer lines are interpreted as arising from two spatially distinct regions within the BLR.

title: Analysis of a coronal hole jet in the chromosphere and the transition region with IRIS data and SDO observations
comment: accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Coronal jets are transient phenomena that occur throughout the solar atmosphere, often triggered by the activation of mini-filaments. Jets are an important field of study, as they are believed to contribute to the mass supply of the solar wind. We study a small-scale solar jet occurring in a low-latitude coronal hole, focusing on traces of the jet eruption to the lower atmosphere, utilizing chromospheric and transition region diagnostics. We also investigate the possible mechanisms and dynamic conditions leading to its onset. We analyze ultraviolet spectra from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph to investigate chromospheric dynamics and their connection to the transition region, using diagnostics of the Mg II k 2796.35 Å and Si IV 1393.75 Å lines, together with non-LTE inversions. We complement this analysis with multiwavelength imaging and magnetograms from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, as well as magnetic field modeling. The analysis of Mg II k and Si IV parameters reveals a coupling between chromospheric and transition region plasma dynamics. Profiles on the jet spire present deeper central reversals, larger peak separations and higher transition region Doppler velocities. The jet initiation is associated with a mini-filament-like structure, preceded by dynamic variations in the photospheric magnetic field. We find single-peaked Mg II k profiles at one of its footpoints, possibly indicating plasma drainage. The presence of a null point and a quasi-separatrix layer suggests that reconnection can play a role in the mini-filament-like structure destabilization and jet eruption. This study suggests that the signature and possibly the origin of coronal jets can be traced down to the chromosphere. The detailed analysis of the Mg II k profiles at the jet spire and the mini-filament-like structure may provide valuable observational constraints for future MHD simulations.

AI.tldr: A small low-latitude coronal-hole jet is traced down to the chromosphere using IRIS Mg II k and Si IV diagnostics plus SDO imaging and magnetic modeling, linking chromospheric/transition-region dynamics to mini-filament destabilization via a null point and quasi-separatrix layer.
AI.motivation: Coronal jets contribute to solar wind mass supply, yet the connection between their eruption signatures and the lower atmosphere, and the mechanisms/conditions for their onset, remain insufficiently characterized observationally.
AI.method: IRIS ultraviolet spectra of Mg II k 2796.35 Å and Si IV 1393.75 Å with non-LTE inversions to diagnose chromospheric and transition region dynamics; complemented by multiwavelength SDO imaging, magnetograms, and magnetic field modeling.
AI.result: Mg II k and Si IV parameters show coupling between chromospheric and transition region plasma dynamics; the jet spire exhibits deeper central reversals, larger peak separations, and higher Si IV Doppler velocities. Jet initiation is associated with a mini-filament-like structure preceded by photospheric magnetic field variations, with single-peaked Mg II k profiles at one footpoint indicating possible plasma drainage. A null point and quasi-separatrix layer support reconnection-driven destabilization.
AI.conclusion: The signature and possibly the origin of coronal jets can be traced down to the chromosphere; the detailed Mg II k profiles at the spire and mini-filament-like structure offer observational constraints for future MHD simulations.

title: Discovering supernovae in the Virgo Cluster during the LSST era
comment: submitted to ApJ -- comments welcome
summary: In the era of unprecedentedly wide, deep and high-cadence sky surveys the chance for discovering new explosive transients in nearby, rich galaxy clusters within hours after explosion is expected to increase dramatically. In this paper we focus on the Virgo cluster ($D \simeq 16.5$ Mpc), and estimate the expected numbers of new, very young supernovae in different sub-structures and galaxy types of the cluster during the proposed lifetime (~10 years) of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) by the Vera Rubin Observatory. These predictions will be tested observationally during the ongoing Shadow-LSST discovery and follow-up program led by University of Arizona in the upcoming years.

AI.tldr: This paper forecasts how many very young supernovae LSST will discover in the Virgo cluster over its ~10-year lifetime, broken down by sub-structure and galaxy type, providing testable predictions for the ongoing Shadow-LSST program.
AI.motivation: Wide, deep, high-cadence surveys are expected to dramatically increase discoveries of explosive transients in nearby rich galaxy clusters within hours of explosion, motivating quantitative predictions.
AI.method: Focusing on the Virgo cluster (D ≈ 16.5 Mpc), the authors estimate expected numbers of very young supernovae across different cluster sub-structures and galaxy types during LSST's proposed ~10-year lifetime.
AI.result: Predicted supernova yields are provided per sub-structure and galaxy type; these predictions will be observationally tested by the University of Arizona-led Shadow-LSST discovery and follow-up program.
AI.conclusion: The forecasts offer a benchmark to validate LSST-era early supernova discovery rates against near-term Shadow-LSST observations.

title: Unexpected Local Enhancement of Chromospheric Moreton Waves on the Sun
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ Letters
summary: Solar eruptions often drive shock waves. When propagating in the solar corona, strong shock waves would leave imprints on the solar surface in the chromosphere, which are called Moreton waves. Moreton waves generally decay as they move away. However, to our knowledge, for the first time we report that a Moreton wave is significantly enhanced midway during propagation, as revealed by the spectroscopic observations from China's first solar satellite, the Chinese H$α$ Solar Explorer. Combining magnetic measurements from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we found that the location of the Moreton wave enhancement corresponds to a magnetic null point at an altitude of $\sim$70 Mm in the corona. It is demonstrated that the unexpected local enhancement of the Moreton wave is due to mode conversion around the magnetic null point, i.e., fast-mode waves are converted to slow-mode waves which are trapped locally. It is further revealed that, even for ordinary Moreton wave fronts, the H$α$ Doppler redshift velocity is positively correlated with the height of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points, implying that these low-lying null points, $\sim$1--7 Mm above the solar surface, facilitate mode conversion with different efficiency, thereby accounting for the spatially inhomogeneous Dopplergram of Moreton wave fronts.

AI.tldr: First spectroscopic detection of a Moreton wave that is significantly enhanced midway during propagation; the enhancement is attributed to fast-to-slow mode conversion at a coronal magnetic null point (~70 Mm altitude), with low-altitude null points (1–7 Mm) explaining inhomogeneous Doppler velocities across ordinary Moreton fronts.
AI.motivation: Moreton waves (chromospheric imprints of coronal shock waves) are generally expected to decay as they propagate. The authors report an anomalous case in which a Moreton wave is significantly enhanced midway, motivating an investigation of the physical mechanism responsible for this unexpected local amplification and of the role of magnetic topology in shaping Moreton wave signatures.
AI.method: Spectroscopic observations from China's first solar satellite, the Chinese Hα Solar Explorer (CHASE), combined with magnetic measurements from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The location of the Moreton wave enhancement is compared with the coronal magnetic field structure to identify a magnetic null point at ~70 Mm altitude; Hα Doppler redshift velocities of Moreton wave fronts are then correlated with the heights of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points (~1–7 Mm).
AI.result: The Moreton wave enhancement coincides with a magnetic null point at ~70 Mm altitude. The local amplification is demonstrated to arise from mode conversion around the magnetic null point: fast-mode waves convert to slow-mode waves that become locally trapped. For ordinary Moreton wave fronts, the Hα Doppler redshift velocity is positively correlated with the height of widespread low-altitude magnetic null points.
AI.conclusion: Local enhancement of a Moreton wave is caused by fast-to-slow mode conversion at a coronal magnetic null point. Low-lying null points (1–7 Mm) facilitate mode conversion with varying efficiency, accounting for the spatially inhomogeneous Dopplergram of Moreton wave fronts. Magnetic null points thus play a key role in modulating Moreton wave propagation and morphology.

title: A neural-network model to find correlations in astrochemical space
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics. Added a previously omitted co-author to the author list. No changes to the scientific content
summary: The detection of new interstellar molecules is central to astrochemistry, and arguably the most transformative development in the field in past decade has been the increase in both number and diversity of detected species. Using natural language processing models, we develop a machine-learning pipeline, similar to other approaches reported in the literature, to connect molecular structures, encoded as chemical strings, and molecular column densities in TMC-1. The workflow generates astrochemically informed embeddings that can be employed in subsequent supervised learning tasks. These representations are used within a neural-network framework to perform column-density regression on both the original molecular inventory and out-of-distribution species. The resulting model achieves mean squared error values of 0.17/0.58 and mean absolute error values of 0.29/0.59, and coefficients of determination of 0.88/0.51 for the train+validation and validation datasets. The latent vectors learned by the model are rich mathematical objects that capture the underlying chemical relations and also the potential interstellar detectability of the molecule. Using these vectors in molecules obtained from systematic permutations of the TMC-1 inventory, we identify several promising candidates for future detection in this cloud, together with a large number of apolar species. By training the model on datasets reflecting different historical epochs of molecular detections in TMC-1, we show that recent molecular detections have substantially reshaped our understanding of interstellar chemistry, in a transformative, rather than incremental, way. Beyond accurate prediction of column-density trends for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution molecules, the latent-space representations produced by the model provide a stepping stone for developing new forms of data-driven astrochemical intuition and exploration.

AI.tldr: A natural-language-processing pipeline learns astrochemically informed embeddings linking chemical strings to TMC-1 column densities, enabling accurate regression for in- and out-of-distribution molecules and identification of candidate interstellar species.
AI.motivation: The rapid increase in number and diversity of detected interstellar molecules makes manual interpretation of molecular inventories increasingly impractical; the authors seek a data-driven way to connect molecular structure to observable column densities and to assess detectability.
AI.method: Natural language processing models encode molecular structures as chemical strings; a machine-learning workflow generates astrochemically informed embeddings, which are then used in a neural-network to regress column densities for both the original TMC-1 molecular inventory and out-of-distribution species. Systematic permutations of the TMC-1 inventory are explored in latent space, and models trained on datasets from different historical epochs of detection are compared.
AI.result: The model achieves MSE of 0.17/0.58, MAE of 0.29/0.59, and R² of 0.88/0.51 on train+validation/validation respectively. The latent vectors capture underlying chemical relations and potential interstellar detectability; permutations of the TMC-1 inventory highlight promising candidate molecules (including many apolar species) for future detection. Epoch-based training shows recent detections have transformed, rather than incrementally shifted, understanding of interstellar chemistry.
AI.conclusion: Beyond accurate column-density prediction for in- and out-distribution molecules, the learned latent representations offer a foundation for data-driven astrochemical intuition and systematic exploration of candidate interstellar species.

title: Slow Massive-Star Formation and the O-Star ZAMS Deficit
comment: Submitted to MNRAS Letters
summary: The scarcity of optically visible O stars near the theoretical zero-age main sequence (ZAMS) has puzzled astronomers for over four decades. We argue that it reflects prolonged accretion. If massive stars assemble over Myr timescales, as the inertial-inflow model predicts, core-hydrogen burning begins before accretion ends, and the stars become optically visible at the end of accretion on a birthline displaced from the standard ZAMS. We test this interpretation by comparing the hot-side envelope of Galactic O stars in the Kiel diagram with accreting stellar-evolution models, adopting a growth law $t_{\mathrm{form}}=τ_0(m_{\mathrm{f}}/60 M_\odot)^α$ with formation time $t_{\mathrm{form}}$ and final mass $m_{\mathrm{f}}$. The resulting birthlines reproduce both the displacement and the high-mass turnover of the observed envelope, with best-fitting parameters $(α,τ_0)=(0.52,4.3\,\mathrm{Myr})$, consistent with independent constraints from the luminosity functions of compact H II regions and OB stars. The two constraints have orthogonal degeneracy directions, so combining them narrows the allowed parameter space, yielding projected 90% confidence intervals $0.43<α<0.60$ and $3.9<τ_0/\mathrm{Myr}<5.0$. The inferred growth law agrees with cloud-scale simulations and the inertial-inflow model, and implies that mass assembly and main-sequence evolution overlap substantially in massive stars, with broader implications for stellar evolution and feedback.

AI.tldr: The absence of ZAMS O stars reflects prolonged accretion; accreting-evolution birthlines with a power-law growth law reproduce the observed hot-side envelope and yield constrained formation parameters.
AI.motivation: The dearth of optically visible O stars near the theoretical ZAMS has been unexplained for over four decades. The authors propose this is a signature of extended (Myr-scale) mass assembly, so that core hydrogen burning starts before accretion finishes and stars appear on a birthline offset from the ZAMS.
AI.method: They compare the hot-side envelope of Galactic O stars in the Kiel diagram with accreting stellar-evolution models, using a growth law t_form = τ0 (m_f/60 M_sun)^α, and combine the fit with independent constraints from luminosity functions of compact H II regions and OB stars.
AI.result: The birthlines reproduce both the displacement and the high-mass turnover of the observed envelope. Best-fit parameters are (α, τ0) = (0.52, 4.3 Myr); combined with orthogonal constraints, projected 90% confidence intervals are 0.43 < α < 0.60 and 3.9 < τ0/Myr < 5.0.
AI.conclusion: The inferred growth law agrees with cloud-scale simulations and the inertial-inflow model, implying substantial overlap between mass assembly and main-sequence evolution in massive stars, with implications for stellar evolution and feedback.

title: Stability of rotation axis of galactic disks in HESTIA suite
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: We have found that in approximately 1/4 of Milky Way or M31 analogues in the HESTIA suite of simulations there is a significant, $>45^\circ$, change in the axis of rotation orientation of the gaseous disk during the last 6 Gyr. In 6 out of 7 such cases the change is likely caused by the accretion of individual satellites, while in one case such a connection is not obvious. All galaxies that underwent a significant change in rotation axis direction also had angular momentum amplitudes below the sample median 6 Gyr ago. Our findings support the idea that last 6~Gyr was a quiet phase of evolution in the LG. On the other hand, the mechanism we detect, that satellites can flip galaxy orientation, can explain the difficulties in identifying correlations between the rotation axis and the orientation of large-scale structure elements.

AI.tldr: About 1/4 of Milky Way/M31 analogues in HESTIA simulations show a >45° change in gas-disk rotation-axis orientation over the last 6 Gyr, mostly driven by satellite accretion, and such flips occur preferentially in galaxies with below-median angular momentum 6 Gyr ago.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to characterize how often and why the rotation-axis orientation of galactic gaseous disks changes in the last 6 Gyr, and to test the picture of a quiet recent evolutionary phase in the Local Group while offering an explanation for the weak observed correlation between galaxy spin axes and large-scale structure orientation.
AI.method: Analysis of Milky Way/M31 analogues in the HESTIA suite of cosmological simulations, measuring changes in the rotation-axis orientation of the gaseous disk over the last 6 Gyr, identifying cases with >45° reorientation, testing for an association with individual satellite accretion events, and comparing angular momentum amplitudes at 6 Gyr ago against the sample median.
AI.result: Approximately 1/4 of the analogues exhibit a significant (>45°) change in gaseous-disk rotation-axis orientation during the last 6 Gyr; in 6 of 7 such cases the change is likely caused by accretion of individual satellites (one case lacks an obvious connection). All galaxies undergoing a significant rotation-axis change had angular momentum amplitudes below the sample median 6 Gyr ago.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the idea that the last ~6 Gyr was a quiet phase of evolution in the Local Group, and the detected mechanism—satellite accretion flipping galaxy orientation—can explain the difficulty in identifying correlations between rotation axes and the orientation of large-scale structure elements.

title: Granulation-driven spectral irradiance variability of Sun-like stars
comment: under review (A&A), 7 pages, 6 Figures
summary: Granulation,caused by convection in low-mass stars like the Sun, introduces small amplitude variations in the stellar brightness on timescales of minutes to hours. Often referred to as flicker or microvariability this signal can impede detecting Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars via stellar transits. Stellar flicker can also introduce uncertainties in determining stellar fundamental parameters and cause errors of up to 10% in the radius determination of transiting exoplanets. Both sources of uncertainties will propagate into planetary transmission spectra and resulting atmospheric retrievals. We present a method for modelling stellar flicker that enables scaling the flicker of Sun-like stars between different wavelengths and passbands to facilitate better solar-stellar comparisons. We use the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic code MURaM to simulate the granulation pattern on a Sun-like star and employ the radiative transfer code MPS-ATLAS for the spectral synthesis of the MURaM output, producing lightcurves of the granulation signal in various wavelengths and at different disc positions. Using these synthetic lightcurves, we establish scaling relations in the time and frequency domain between different wavelengths and passbands routinely used in stellar observations, such as the Kepler and TESS space telescopes. We find that the variability caused by granulation is very well correlated across wavelengths from 300 to 6000 nm, enabling scalings from one wavelength regime to another. We present the scaling sensitivities in different passbands and wavelength regimes that can be used to facilitate solar-stellar comparisons and help estimate stellar flicker in observations using photometric passbands and low-resolution transmission spectra.

AI.tldr: This work models stellar granulation ("flicker") using MURaM 3D radiative MHD simulations combined with MPS-ATLAS spectral synthesis, and derives wavelength/passband scaling relations for the flicker signal of Sun-like stars to support solar–stellar comparisons and mitigate photometric noise in exoplanet studies.
AI.motivation: Granulation-driven microvariability in Sun-like stars introduces brightness variations on minute-to-hour timescales that hamper transit detection of Earth-sized planets, bias stellar radius (and hence transiting exoplanet radius) determinations by up to ~10%, and propagate into transmission spectra and atmospheric retrievals. A means of relating flicker across wavelengths/passbands is needed for robust solar–stellar comparison and error mitigation.
AI.method: The authors use the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic code MURaM to simulate the granulation pattern of a Sun-like star, and apply the radiative transfer code MPS-ATLAS for spectral synthesis of the MURaM output. This produces synthetic lightcurves of the granulation signal across multiple wavelengths and at different disc positions. From these lightcurves they establish scaling relations—in both time and frequency domains—between different wavelengths and passbands routinely used in observations (e.g., Kepler and TESS).
AI.result: The granulation-induced variability is found to be highly correlated across wavelengths from 300 to 6000 nm, permitting scaling from one wavelength regime to another. Scaling sensitivities are presented for various passbands and wavelength regimes.
AI.conclusion: Flicker variability can be reliably rescaled across wavelengths and photometric passbands, enabling solar–stellar comparisons and estimation of stellar flicker in observations using photometric passbands and low-resolution transmission spectra.

title: EP J062132.0+623837: A Multi-wavelength Study of a Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Discovered by Einstein Probe
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: EP J062132.0+623837 is a new X-ray source identified in 14-day binned survey data from the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe (EP). Subsequent X-ray observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board EP localized the source to the central region of the galaxy 2MASX J06213207+6238390 at $z=0.084$. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the multi-wavelength data for this object. During the FXT and Swift/XRT follow-up, the source remained X-ray active, with observed luminosities of $(3-9)\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and its X-ray spectra were well described by power-law models with photon indices of $Γ\sim1.5$. The optical spectrum of the host galaxy clearly reveals a broad-line active galactic nucleus (AGN) exhibiting significantly enhanced broad Balmer emission lines compared to an archival spectrum obtained four years earlier, thereby marking a changing-look transition from Type 1.8 to Type 1.5. Furthermore, long-term optical and mid-infrared light curves indicate that the nucleus underwent dramatic brightening around 2010 and has since shown substantial variability. Given the spatial coincidence and multi-wavelength behavior, we identify EP J062132.0+623837 as a changing-look AGN, initially detected by EP and subsequently confirmed to exhibit large-amplitude variability across multiple bands. This case study demonstrates the great potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys for discovering changing-look AGNs, paving a new avenue for their systematic identification as a powerful complement to ongoing optical surveys.

AI.tldr: EP J062132.0+623837 is identified as a new X-ray source by Einstein Probe and confirmed as a changing-look AGN in the nucleus of 2MASX J06213207+6238390 (z=0.084), exhibiting a Type 1.8-to-1.5 transition and multi-band large-amplitude variability.
AI.motivation: Wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys offer a largely unexploited route to systematically discover changing-look AGNs, complementing ongoing optical surveys. This work tests that potential on a newly detected EP source.
AI.method: Analysis of 14-day binned Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) survey data from EP, followed by FXT and Swift/XRT X-ray follow-up spectroscopy (power-law fits), optical spectroscopy of the host galaxy compared with an archival spectrum from four years earlier, and long-term optical and mid-infrared light-curve analysis.
AI.result: The source remained X-ray active with luminosities of (3-9)x10^43 erg/s and photon indices Gamma~1.5. The optical spectrum shows a broad-line AGN with significantly enhanced broad Balmer lines relative to the archival spectrum, marking a Type 1.8-to-1.5 changing-look transition. Long-term optical and mid-IR light curves reveal dramatic nuclear brightening around 2010 followed by substantial variability.
AI.conclusion: EP J062132.0+623837 is a changing-look AGN, first detected by EP and confirmed through large-amplitude multi-wavelength variability. The case demonstrates the strong potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys as a systematic discovery channel for changing-look AGNs, complementary to optical surveys.

title: Magnetic Activity as a Driver of Low-gravity-like Spectral Morphology in Late-M Dwarfs
comment: 39 pages, 13 figures, 10 tables
summary: We present a systematic investigation of the connection between magnetic activity and the low-surface-gravity-like near-infrared spectral morphology of late-M dwarfs. Our sample includes TRAPPIST-1 observed with JWST NIRISS/SOSS and 22 late-M dwarfs observed with IRTF/SpeX, together with flare observations from K2, TESS, JWST NIRISS/SOSS, and literature-reported X-ray luminosities. Using one-component PHOENIX/NewEra spectral modeling, we find that all targets are better reproduced by lower-surface-gravity model spectra than by models with the expected high gravities of field late-M dwarfs. The retrieved surface gravities moderately correlate with independently measured gravity-sensitive spectral indices, with the strongest trends seen for FeH$_z$ at 0.998~$μ$m and FeH$_J$ at 1.2~$μ$m, both showing statistically significant Pearson and Spearman correlations with $p<0.005$. They also show strong anti-correlations with flare luminosity and X-ray luminosity: for both relations, Pearson and Spearman coefficients are $<-0.9$, with $p \leq 1.0\times10^{-4}$, indicating that more active stars tend to have spectra favoring lower-gravity morphologies. Time-series spectra of TRAPPIST-1 during two large flares show no clear short-timescale variations in selected photospheric indices, suggesting that persistent small-scale magnetic activity may play a more important role than large flares in modifying the photospheric temperature--pressure structure. A simplified radiative-transfer experiment further shows that activity-associated heating can produce lower-gravity-like spectral features even when the input surface gravity is fixed. Our results suggest that underestimated surface gravities in late-M dwarfs may reflect atmospheres modified by frequent, small-scale magnetic activity, such as microflares, producing emergent spectra that mimic lower-gravity morphology.

AI.tldr: Magnetic activity in late-M dwarfs modifies atmospheres so that spectra mimic lower-gravity morphology, explaining systematically underestimated surface gravities.
AI.motivation: Field late-M dwarfs systematically yield lower surface gravities than expected from evolutionary models, and the cause is unclear; the authors test whether magnetic activity drives this near-infrared (NIR) low-gravity-like spectral morphology.
AI.method: Sample: TRAPPIST-1 (JWST NIRISS/SOSS) plus 22 late-M dwarfs (IRTF/SpeX), with flare data from K2, TESS, JWST NIRISS/SOSS and literature X-ray luminosities. One-component PHOENIX/NewEra spectral fitting retrieves surface gravity; results compared with gravity-sensitive indices (FeH_z at 0.998 μm, FeH_J at 1.2 μm) and with activity indicators. Time-series spectra during two large TRAPPIST-1 flares probe short-timescale variability, and a simplified radiative-transfer experiment tests heating effects at fixed gravity.
AI.result: All targets are better fit by lower-gravity models than by expected field gravities. Retrieved gravities correlate moderately with FeH_z and FeH_J indices (p<0.005) and strongly anti-correlate with flare and X-ray luminosities (Pearson and Spearman <-0.9, p<=1e-4). No clear short-timescale changes in photospheric indices appear during two large flares. Radiative-transfer heating reproduces low-gravity-like features at fixed input gravity.
AI.conclusion: Underestimated surface gravities in late-M dwarfs likely reflect atmospheres modified by persistent small-scale magnetic activity (e.g., microflares), not large flares, producing spectra that mimic lower-gravity morphology.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning for JWST Galaxy Images and Low Resolution Spectra
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for the NeurIPS 2026 RPS Workshop. Comments welcome. Detailed descriptions of the data, model training and additional benchmarks are included in the appendix (11 pages, 4 figures)
summary: A self-supervised multimodal model recovers galaxy stellar masses from sparse JWST data that lack the multi-band coverage required by traditional SED fitting. We train on single-band F150W imaging paired with observed-frame 1-2 $μ$m PRISM spectra and obtain a joint image-spectrum representation that recovers stellar mass at $1<z\le3$ with $R^2 \sim 0.9$ and $σ_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.24$ dex; cross-modal CLIP alignment further raises single-modality performance by $ΔR^2 = +0.04$ (imaging) and $+0.09$ (spectroscopy), narrowing the gap to joint-modality inference. The code and documentation are available at \href{https://github.com/2003cy/neurips2026_ssl_jwst}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised multimodal model (image + spectrum, with CLIP-style cross-modal alignment) estimates galaxy stellar masses from sparse single-band JWST/F150W data, achieving R² ≈ 0.9 and σ_NMAD = 0.24 dex at 1 < z ≤ 3 without requiring multi-band SED coverage.
AI.motivation: Traditional stellar-mass estimation relies on multi-band SED fitting, but much JWST data lack sufficient multi-band coverage (e.g., only a single band like F150W available), making standard SED fitting infeasible. The paper aims to recover stellar masses under such sparse-data conditions.
AI.method: A self-supervised multimodal model trained on single-band F150W imaging paired with observed-frame 1–2 μm PRISM spectra, learning a joint image–spectrum representation. Cross-modal CLIP alignment is additionally used to regularize and align the per-modality embeddings.
AI.result: Joint image–spectrum inference recovers stellar mass at 1 < z ≤ 3 with R² ~ 0.9 and σ_NMAD = 0.24 dex. Cross-modal CLIP alignment improves single-modality performance by ΔR² = +0.04 for imaging and +0.09 for spectroscopy, narrowing the gap to joint-modality inference. Code and documentation are released.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised cross-modal pretraining enables robust stellar-mass inference from sparse single-band JWST photometry, and CLIP-style alignment transfers spectral information into each individual modality, making single-band imaging alone a viable mass estimator.

title: A Catalog of Spectral Properties for DESI DR1 Quasars
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, and 2 tables. Preprint version; comments and feedback are welcome
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is carrying out a five-year spectroscopic survey designed to map the large-scale structure of the Universe and obtain spectra for millions of galaxies and quasars over a wide redshift range. We present a value-added catalog of spectral properties for 1,717,774 unique quasars (1,774,723 spectra) in the DESI Data Release 1. We perform a uniform spectral decomposition of the quasar continuum, host galaxy emission (at $z<1$), and \FeII\ emission, and measure the line properties of major broad and narrow emission lines from Ly$α$ to H$α$ covered by DESI spectra. We also provide single-epoch black hole mass estimates (from H$β$, \MgII, and \CIV), bolometric luminosities, and Eddington ratios for these quasars. We provide systemic redshifts that account for the intrinsic velocity shifts of individual lines; they agree with the DESI pipeline redshifts to within 500~km s$^{-1}$ for 88.6\% of the sample, and are most useful at $z>1$ where the pipeline redshift is heavily constrained by blueshifted high-ionization lines. We also provide local fits to several optical coronal lines, including \NeV~$\lambda3426$, [\ion{Fe}{7}]~$\lambda5722$, [\ion{Fe}{7}]~$\lambda6088$, and [\ion{Fe}{11}]~$\lambda7893$. We show that several emission-line ratios, including those involving coronal lines, vary systematically with Eddington ratio. The catalog is intended as a community resource for studies of quasar demographics, black hole accretion, emission-line physics, and the connection between the broad-, coronal-, and narrow-line regions.

AI.tldr: A value-added catalog of spectral properties for 1.72 million unique quasars from DESI Data Release 1, providing uniform spectral decomposition, emission-line measurements, black hole masses, bolometric luminosities, Eddington ratios, and improved systemic redshifts.
AI.motivation: DESI's large spectroscopic survey of quasars requires a homogeneous, value-added characterization of spectral properties that goes beyond the pipeline products, enabling studies of quasar demographics, black hole accretion, and emission-line physics.
AI.method: Uniform spectral decomposition of quasar continuum, host-galaxy emission (z<1), and Fe II emission; measurement of broad and narrow emission lines from Ly-alpha to H-alpha; single-epoch black hole mass estimates from H-beta, Mg II, and C IV; bolometric luminosities and Eddington ratios; systemic redshifts accounting for intrinsic line velocity shifts; local fits to optical coronal lines ([Ne V] 3426, [Fe VII] 5722/6088, [Fe XI] 7893).
AI.result: Catalog contains 1,717,774 unique quasars (1,774,723 spectra). Systemic redshifts agree with DESI pipeline redshifts within 500 km/s for 88.6% of the sample and are most useful at z>1. Several emission-line ratios, including those involving coronal lines, vary systematically with Eddington ratio.
AI.conclusion: The catalog serves as a community resource for studies of quasar demographics, black hole accretion, emission-line physics, and the connection between broad-, coronal-, and narrow-line regions.

title: SpecLess: A Multi Survey Python Package for Machine Learning Classification of Galaxy Morphology and Activity from Photometry
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. Submitted to Astronomy & Computing. SpecLess v0.3.0. Open source Python package available at https://github.com/uzayyaydiin/SpecLess
summary:
Broad band photometry enables scalable galaxy classification without spectroscopy at inference time, yet strong within survey performance may not transfer when the same galaxies are measured by another survey. We present SpecLess, an open source Python package implementing two photometric classification tasks: high confidence Galaxy Zoo 1 elliptical and spiral morphologies, and four SDSS spectroscopic activity reference classes (starforming, starburst, Seyfert, and LINER). Using SDSS+AllWISE, KiDS+VIKING, and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys photometry, survey specific XGBoost classifiers achieve held out macro F1 scores of 0.9332 (SDSS; 35,554 galaxies) and 0.9237 (KiDS; 3,269) for morphology, and 0.7637 (SDSS; 16,931) and 0.7398 (DESI; 11,975) for activity. Starforming and starburst references are recovered more effectively than Seyfert and LINER, while feature ablations reveal complementary contributions from optical and mid infrared photometry.
  We quantify catalogue dependence using separately trained common feature models evaluated on matched galaxies with identical labels and data partitions. Relative to target trained models, macro F1 deficits are 0.0153 (SDSS to KiDS) and 0.0354 (KiDS to SDSS) for morphology (12,301 galaxies; 20 splits), and 0.0660 (SDSS to DESI) and 0.0406 (DESI to SDSS) for activity (11,975 test galaxies). Colour only refits, additive corrections, and optical infrared substitutions reveal direction dependent sensitivity without consistently recovering target trained performance.
  SpecLess v0.3.0 distributes four pretrained, survey specific classifiers through a unified Python interface. The package provides a reproducible baseline for photometric galaxy classification across multiple surveys while establishing an extensible, open source foundation for future developments in classification methods and photometric catalogue support.

AI.tldr: SpecLess is an open source Python package that trains survey-specific broad band photometric classifiers for galaxy morphology (elliptical/spiral) and activity (starforming, starburst, Seyfert, LINER), and quantifies how much performance degrades when transferring across SDSS, KiDS, and DESI catalogues.
AI.motivation: Broad band photometry enables scalable galaxy classification without spectroscopy at inference, but strong within-survey performance may not transfer when the same galaxies are observed by another survey. The paper aims to quantify this catalogue dependence and provide a reproducible open source baseline.
AI.method: Two classification tasks using Galaxy Zoo 1 morphologies and SDSS spectroscopic activity references. Survey-specific XGBoost classifiers trained on SDSS+AllWISE, KiDS+VIKING, and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys photometry. Transfer is tested with separately trained common-feature models evaluated on matched galaxies with identical labels and data partitions, plus colour-only refits, additive corrections, and optical/infrared substitutions; feature ablations assess modality contributions.
AI.result: Held-out macro F1: morphology 0.9332 (SDSS, 35,554 galaxies) and 0.9237 (KiDS, 3,269); activity 0.7637 (SDSS, 16,931) and 0.7398 (DESI, 11,975). Starforming/starburst are recovered better than Seyfert/LINER. Cross-survey deficits relative to target-trained models: morphology 0.0153 (SDSS→KiDS) and 0.0354 (KiDS→SDSS) on 12,301 galaxies over 20 splits; activity 0.0660 (SDSS→DESI) and 0.0406 (DESI→SDSS) on 11,975 test galaxies. Corrections show direction-dependent sensitivity without consistently recovering target-trained performance; ablation shows complementary optical and mid-infrared contributions.
AI.conclusion: SpecLess v0.3.0 distributes four pretrained survey-specific classifiers via a unified Python interface, offering a reproducible cross-survey baseline and an extensible open source foundation for future classification methods and photometric catalogue support.

title: Odd radio circle J1555+2726: Observational evidence for shock re-acceleration of fossil plasma
comment: 11 pages (+3 pages appendix). Resubmitted to A&A after referee's report
summary: Context. Odd radio circles (ORCs) are peculiar extragalactic sources recently discovered. They are characterised by one or more bright rings extending on scales of hundreds of kiloparsecs, and are filled with fainter emission. A massive elliptical galaxy lies at the centre of ORCs. While their formation mechanism is debated, a shock is plausibly involved. Aims. We aim to constrain the nature of ORC J1555+2726 (ORC4) through the analysis of its morphological and spectral properties. Methods. We utilised Low Frequency ARray (LOFAR), upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT), and MeerKAT radio data at 50-1284 MHz to obtain images and spectral index maps at high resolution and sensitivity. Results. Both the resolution and observing frequency affect the observed morphology. In particular, the brightness contrast between the ring and the filling emission becomes progressively smoother from higher to lower frequencies. We measured an integrated spectrum of slope $α=1.06\pm 0.03$, a radio power of $P_{\rm 150}= (5.4\pm 0.5)\times 10^{25} \; {\rm W \; Hz^{-1}}$ at 150 MHz, and a radial spectral flattening down to $α\sim0.5$ at the ring location. However, we inferred a negative (convex) spectral curvature and a peculiar spectral shape in radio colour-colour diagrams, which imply spectral flattening towards high frequencies. These properties cannot be explained by shock acceleration of thermal particles and standard ageing. Conclusions. The observed features suggest that a mixture of electrons with different spectra coexist within ORC4 volume, likely associated with shock re-acceleration of a fossil relativistic reservoir. The ring emission is plausibly dominated by higher-energy electrons re-accelerated at the shock front, while lower-energy re-accelerated electrons are more uniformly distributed across the whole source (possibly ellipsoidal) volume.

AI.tldr: Multi-frequency (50–1284 MHz) LOFAR/uGMRT/MeerKAT analysis of ORC J1555+2726 reveals frequency- and resolution-dependent morphology, an integrated spectral index α=1.06±0.03, radial spectral flattening (α~0.5) at the ring, and convex spectral curvature, interpreted as shock re-acceleration of a fossil relativistic electron reservoir.
AI.motivation: Odd radio circles (ORCs) are recently discovered extragalactic sources with bright rings on hundreds-of-kpc scales, filled with fainter emission and centered on massive elliptical galaxies. Their formation mechanism is debated, with shocks plausibly involved. The authors aim to constrain the nature of ORC J1555+2726 (ORC4) via its morphological and spectral properties.
AI.method: The authors used LOFAR, upgraded GMRT, and MeerKAT radio data spanning 50–1284 MHz to produce high-resolution, high-sensitivity images and spectral index maps of ORC4, examining how resolution and observing frequency affect the observed morphology and measuring integrated and spatially resolved spectral properties.
AI.result: Both resolution and observing frequency affect morphology: the brightness contrast between the ring and the filling emission becomes progressively smoother from higher to lower frequencies. They measured an integrated spectrum of slope α=1.06±0.03, a radio power P_150=(5.4±0.5)×10^25 W Hz^-1 at 150 MHz, and a radial spectral flattening down to α~0.5 at the ring location. They inferred a negative (convex) spectral curvature and a peculiar spectral shape in radio colour–colour diagrams, implying spectral flattening towards high frequencies—features inconsistent with shock acceleration of thermal particles and standard ageing.
AI.conclusion: The observed features suggest a mixture of electrons with different spectra coexists within the ORC4 volume, likely associated with shock re-acceleration of a fossil relativistic reservoir. Ring emission is plausibly dominated by higher-energy electrons re-accelerated at the shock front, while lower-energy re-accelerated electrons are more uniformly distributed across the whole (possibly ellipsoidal) source volume.
